In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/substrate-gap.ts, inside resolveSubstrateGapWrite, refuse to CREATE a gap whose summary merely echoes the summary of the gap it claims to decompose.

WHY. A summary beginning with the decompose prefix followed by an id and a colon is supposed to be a decomposition of that parent gap. Measured on the live store: of 50 such gaps, all 50 have a resolvable parent, and 33 of them (66 percent) carry an inner body that is prefix-identical to the parent's inner body once the decompose prefix is recursively stripped from both. Five are byte-identical. The echoed bodies cluster at exactly 399 to 400 characters, which is the truncation point, so the operation being performed is: copy the parent summary, truncate it, mint a new id. A control confirms this is real and not an artifact of the comparison: the other 17 carry materially different text, so the path can produce new content when it works.

THE HARM. Each echo starts a new gap id with its failed-attempt counter reset to zero, so the landability seal that fires at eight attempts with zero lands never fires; one observed chain burned fourteen attempts across four ids, each capped at four. And because the echo copies the parent's instruction text forward verbatim, a recorded failure lesson can never correct a defect that lives in that instruction text: one observed chain records a lesson saying the changed symbol has zero callers and cannot execute, while carrying forward the parent instruction that forbids wiring the symbol in. The lesson and the instruction contradict, and the instruction wins on every retry.

THE CHANGE. resolveSubstrateGapWrite already loads the full gap set before deciding create-versus-update, in order to dedup by gap class, so the parent row is already in hand and no new read is needed. When the incoming write is a CREATE, and its summary matches the decompose prefix, resolve the named parent from that already-loaded set, strip the decompose prefix recursively from both summaries, and if the incoming inner body is a prefix of the parent's inner body, refuse the create and return a structured error naming the parent id. A child that adds no text cannot by construction be a decomposition. Leave updates and non-decompose creates untouched.

This is the same chokepoint, and the same shape of guard, as the summary-preservation logic already present in that function.

The semantic gate accepts an adversarial refuter's verdict without ever executing the counter-example that verdict rests on. Observed 2026-09-06 refusing a fix that was measurably correct.

THE INCIDENT. A one-line change to a deterministic refusal predicate was composed correctly and applied cleanly. The semantic gate returned addresses:false, recorded 'adversarial refuters agreed 2/2 (conf 1.00, 0.90)', and rolled the change back. Its stated reason named two concrete counter-examples it believed the change failed to handle. Both were wrong: running the changed predicate against the refuter's own two examples showed it handles both correctly. Measured on the ten-case discriminating suite, the old predicate is wrong on four cases and the new one on zero. Verified end to end against the real exported function rather than the predicate alone: a 358-mutant metamorphic sweep drops from 43 escapes to 27, the two hazardous forms flip from passing to refused, the legitimate exemptions stay exempt so the gate does not over-fire, and typecheck exits zero.

WHY THIS CLASS MATTERS. A refuter that cites a specific input is making a mechanically checkable claim, and nothing checks it. The verdict was delivered at confidence 1.00, so confidence carries no information about whether the cited example was ever evaluated. This is the mirror image of an already-recorded incident where the same gate graded a broken commit as reaching and the correct follow-up fix as failing: taken together they show the judge erring in both directions on the same kind of change, which is what one expects from a layer that reads a diff and never runs it.

THE COST IS ASYMMETRIC AND HIDDEN. A false refusal produces no artifact, no landed commit, and no penalty anywhere. It looks identical to a change that was never attempted, so a gate that wrongly refuses is invisible to every progress measure while a gate that wrongly accepts eventually shows up as a defect. That asymmetry means false refusals accumulate silently.

REMEDY DIRECTION for the semantic-gate path in the file named by edit_site: when a refusal reason contains a concrete literal input and the change under review modifies a deterministic predicate, evaluate that literal against both the old and the new predicate before accepting the refusal, and record the outcome on the trace. If the new predicate handles every cited literal correctly, the refusal is not supported by its own stated evidence and must be downgraded rather than applied. At minimum, persist the cited literals to the trace so the claim is auditable after the fact, because at present the reason string is the only record and nothing consumes it.

FALSIFIER. Count refusals whose reason contains a quoted literal, and for the subset where the change modified a regex or string predicate, evaluate the literal against the post-change predicate. Any case where the cited literal is handled correctly is a refusal unsupported by its own evidence. This gap is closed when that count is reported rather than unknown.

  const dispatchResponse = await fetch(RUN_GOAL_URL, {

Behaviour of the new block.

Look up the learned statistics for the template named by the existing SCAFFOLD_TEMPLATE_ID constant. Build the base URL from `process.env.ACTIVITY_API_ENDPOINT`, defaulting to "http://127.0.0.1:8080" when unset, and request the path "/v2/activities/templates?limit=200". Send `Content-Type: application/json`, and when `process.env.METABOB_API_KEY` is a non-empty string also send an `Authorization` header of the word ApiKey followed by a space and that key. Parse the JSON body and scan its `templates` array for the entry whose identifier matches SCAFFOLD_TEMPLATE_ID after removing a leading "activity:" prefix and, if present, an enclosing pair of the mathematical angle brackets U+27E8 and U+27E9.

From the matched entry, read the two numbers `metrics.thompson_alpha` and `metrics.thompson_beta`. Take them from the nested `metrics` object only. The template object also carries a top-level `thompson_alpha`, which is a fixed prior of 1 and carries no learning; reading it instead would make this check meaningless.

Compute total as alpha plus beta and rate as alpha divided by total. Decline the invocation only when total is at least 100 AND rate is below 0.01. In every other situation proceed exactly as the file does today and call fetch as before. That includes: no matching template, a network error, an unparseable body, or either statistic missing or not finite. Never decline on missing data, because a template with no history would otherwise become permanently unreachable.

When declining, skip the fetch entirely, write one console line naming the template id together with alpha, beta and rate, and return the same result object the function already returns, reusing the shape constant and the already-computed vessel_name, port, advertised_shapes_literal, description, commit_message, pr_title and pr_body values. Set dispatched_at to the current time as an ISO string. Set dispatch_response to an object recording that the dispatch was declined, a reason of "posterior_decisively_negative", and the observed template id, alpha, beta and rate. The dispatch_response property is declared as unknown, so no interface change is required.

Motivation for the reviewer. This resolver invokes a template by hardcoded identifier directly against run-goal, which skips activity selection completely. The template it names currently carries a learned alpha near 6 against a beta near 8585, one success against roughly 7980 failures, and every one of its 2320 stored executions is a failure — yet it continues to be invoked, because nothing on this path ever reads that record. This change makes the resolver read it.

In repos/ias-executor-ts/src/hosts/goal-host.ts, the runGoal path already knows when a caller has bypassed activity selection, and records that fact, but never consults the bypassed template's learned posterior before executing it.

THE MARKER ALREADY EXISTS. When a caller passes an explicit target template id, runGoal skips the recommender entirely and stamps the resulting trace with a field recording the originally-requested template. Its own comment states that this recording is unconditional in the bypass path and absent when the recommender ran. So every bypass in the fleet passes through this one function and is positively identified there. A drift detector already reads that field, but only to compare requested against selected; nothing reads it to ask whether the requested template is worth running at all.

WHAT THIS COSTS, MEASURED. The template development-vessel:scaffold-and-publish-vessel carries a learned posterior of alpha 6.05 against beta 8601.67 - one success against 7996 failures, a success rate of 0.000125 - and it is not deprecated. Its trace rows number 2340 and every one of them is a failure. It executed twice more during a thirty minute observation window while this gap was being written. In a sample of the last 49 terminal dispatches, 33 of the 40 that produced no learning signal at all were this one template. The evidence against it is overwhelming, it is stored in the right table, it is updated continuously, and the dispatch path never looks at it.

WHY THE BYPASS ITSELF IS NOT THE BUG. Callers pin a target deliberately, and the code says why: to stop selection from misrouting a goal to some unrelated high-alpha template. That reason is sound and the pinning should stay. What is missing is that pinning a target currently means skipping the evidence as well as skipping the choice. Those are separable. A caller can be allowed to say which template it wants while still being refused when that template has a decisively negative record.

THE SHAPE OF THE CHANGE. In the bypass branch, before executing, look up the pinned template's learned posterior and refuse the execution when the evidence is both substantial and decisively negative - for example at least one hundred combined observations and a success rate below one percent. Proceed in every other case, including any failure to obtain the posterior. Proceeding on absence of evidence is essential: a template with no history must stay reachable or the guard becomes a permanent block on anything new. Read the learned posterior from the nested metrics object on the template record, never the top level field of the same name, which is the static prior and is always one.

VERIFICATION THAT WOULD ACTUALLY SETTLE IT. Not a typecheck, and not a unit test over the predicate. Record the arm's trace row count, leave the substrate running, and confirm the count stops increasing while a healthy pinned template continues to dispatch normally. Two guards for this same defect have already been written and both were inert: one matched on a template field that does not exist, and one was placed on a resolver that the traffic does not pass through. Both typechecked, and one of them passed the semantic gate and a cutover. A patch that cannot be shown to change the count is not a fix.

[narrowed from route-edit-8487fc68] In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/substrate-gap.ts, add a write-time guard that rejects a decomposition gap which only repeats its parent.

The insertion point is the end of the `if (existingIdx < 0) { ... }` block whose body is this single statement, which occurs exactly once in the file and is indented with FOUR spaces:

    existingIdx = gaps.findIndex((g) => hasClassifiableId(g) && g.status !== "closed" && gapClassKey(g.id) === classKey);

Match that line exactly as written, including its four-space indentation. Do not confuse it with the similar `let existingIdx = gaps.findIndex((g) => g.id === gap.id);` earlier in the same function, which is a different statement and must not be touched.

Place the new code immediately after the closing brace of that block.

What the guard must do. It applies only when the write would create a new row, meaning `existingIdx` is still less than zero after that block. Take the incoming `gap.summary`. If it does not match the case-insensitive pattern of the literal words "investigate and decompose gap", then a parent identifier, then a colon, do nothing further and let execution continue as before. Otherwise capture that parent identifier and look it up in the already-loaded `gaps` array by exact id match. If no such row exists, again do nothing and continue.

When the parent row is found, derive an inner body from each of the two summaries by repeatedly removing that same leading "investigate and decompose gap <id>:" pattern and trimming whitespace, looping at most ten times because a parent summary may itself carry the prefix. Compare the two inner bodies case-insensitively. If the incoming inner body is not empty and the parent inner body starts with it, return early with shape "structuredError" whose body has resolver set to "substrateGap_write", failure_mode set to "decompose_child_echoes_parent", and a detail string naming the parent id and the two inner-body lengths.

Every other write proceeds unchanged: updates, ordinary creates, and decomposition children that genuinely add text beyond their parent.

Rationale for reviewers: the function already loads the whole `gaps` array before choosing between create and update so that it can deduplicate by gap class, so the parent record is already in memory and the guard needs no additional read. A child whose body is merely a leading fragment of its parent's body has contributed no new content and therefore cannot be a decomposition. On the live store 33 of 50 such children are exactly that, and their bodies cluster at the 400-character truncation boundary.

Change nothing else, and edit no other file.

A decisively negative learned posterior is not sufficient evidence to stop an activity. The posterior is inflated by roughly two orders of magnitude for the highest volume arms, and the live trace store cannot corroborate it because the store lost its own history. No interface exposes a trustworthy execution count that a decision point could cross check against.

WHY THIS MATTERS NOW. A guard refuses a pinned dispatch when the target's learned posterior is decisively negative, defined as at least one hundred combined observations and a success rate below one percent. It works and it is measured: the arm it was built for held flat at 2345 trace rows across a twelve minute window while the fleet executed sixteen other things. The obvious next step is to apply the same rule to selection everywhere. That step is unsafe, and this gap records why and what would make it safe.

THE RULE SCORED AGAINST REAL TRACES. Thirteen arms meet the criterion. Five are correct refusals, having real executions and zero successes. Seven are unfalsifiable, having no rows in the live store at all. One is catastrophically wrong: the authentication resolve arm, whose posterior reports 401711 observations at a success rate of two point four nine parts per million, while the live store holds 2652 executions of which 607 succeeded, a real success rate of twenty three percent. The posterior is inflated about one hundred and fifty one times, matching the chain credit inflation recorded elsewhere. Generalising the rule to selection would refuse a working authentication path on a number wrong by five orders of magnitude. The guard is safe today only because it fires on the pinned dispatch path and exactly one arm is currently pinned.

WHY CORROBORATION IS HARD, STATED CORRECTLY. There are two execution tables and they are not two ledgers. The table named execution is authoritative and always written; it holds 36125 rows, is capped at one hundred and fifty thousand, and carries about fifteen thousand five hundred rows since the first of September. The table named activity execution traces is a decommissioned dual write shadow: the write is gated on a dual write flag whose default is false and which is unset in the live process environment, and it holds zero rows created after the first of August. It is a pre August archive that will never gain another row. Both tables use both key conventions, so any join must strip a leading activity prefix and angle brackets rather than switching between forms.

The consequence is that of the two hundred and four arms carrying at least one hundred posterior observations, forty eight appear in both tables, twenty four only in the live store, seventy nine only in the archive, and fifty three in neither. Seventy nine arms therefore last executed before August. The live store itself lost history: an inline measurement in the trace store code records it reaching three hundred and three thousand rows against the one hundred and fifty thousand cap and being undrainable, because the table carries sixteen indexes and sustains only about zero point two deletes per second against roughly one thousand inserts per hour. It now holds nothing before the first of August, so it was truncated. That is why fifty three arms have no rows anywhere, and it is why trace absence is much weaker evidence than trace presence.

A CONTROL THAT MUST ACCOMPANY ANY IMPLEMENTATION. A per arm reading of zero successes is meaningful only where the success field is live and where success sampling is off. In the live store the status field reads success on 24156 rows, which is sixty seven percent, so the field is live here. A success sampler also exists in the trace write path: failures are never sampled, but successes in named families are dropped, and the early return happens after the shadow insert and before the authoritative insert. On this deployment it is inert, because the sampled family list is unset and the keep rate defaults to one. Any implementation must re check both, because an active sampler would bias every zero success reading toward zero.

A SECOND HAZARD. A datetime comparison in a query silently discards its conjunct partner even when both are parenthesised. Filtering on an activity identifier together with a created at bound returned 10853 rows, precisely the count for the date bound alone, for an arm holding only 2652 rows in total. The same query filtering on an activity identifier together with a status value returns 607 and is correct. Only the arithmetic impossibility exposed this. Any implementation must filter by date and then narrow client side.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS. Expose one trustworthy execution count at the decision point, computed from the live store alone, since a decision point must not depend on a decommissioned table. Then change the refusal criterion from a bare posterior rate to a conjunction: the arm must have live recorded executions, those executions must show zero successes, and there must be enough of them. A minimum real trace count is required because the posterior can be inflated about one hundred and fifty times, so an arm crossing the hundred observation threshold may rest on a single real trace; one of the five correct refusals sits at zero successes over exactly one execution. Without a minimum, a single unlucky failure seals an arm permanently, which is the immortality defect inverted.

Finally, treat the mismatch itself as signal. An arm carrying at least one hundred posterior observations and zero rows in the live store has a posterior that is by definition unbacked by current evidence. That describes the fifty three and the seven. Such an arm should be marked stale rather than failing, and the correct response is to seek fresh evidence, not to refuse it on the strength of a number nothing can corroborate.

Two defects, one field. (1) ROOT CAUSE OF BLINDNESS: activity-api/src/routes/goal-paths.ts:430 runs accumulateEndpointShapes only when endpoint_output_shapes is `undefined`. goal-host's recordGoalPath (goal-host-vessel/src/index.ts:5777) always SENDS the key, as [] for a satisfier-only walk, so the fallback never fires and the row records []. The donor query is `WHERE endpoint_output_shapes CONTAINSANY $target_shapes`, and an empty array matches nothing, so the pathway is invisible as a donor however often it succeeded. Measured: 8,314 of 9,853 pathways (84.4%) are shape-blind; 1,958 of those succeeded at least once. (2) WRONG SOURCE: accumulateEndpointShapes unions the DECLARED output_shapes of path activities. Scored against the 1,539 rows carrying recorded shapes, stratified by era: declared-union produced a SUPERSET or mixed label in 95/297 cases before 2026-08-26 and 390/1149 since (~33%). Deriving instead from execution.output_impulse_shapes (what runs observably produced), unioned with satisfier:<shape> decoding, produced 0 supersets and 0 mixed across both eras (n=853 derivable). The direction matters because cover is donor-covers-goal (goal-paths.ts:1065, |have INTERSECT target|/|target|): a subset label only misses a donor, but a superset label both puts the pathway in CONTAINSANY range for a shape it never produced and earns it cover credit -- a confidently wrong donor. Caveat: declared-union wrote some of the rows it was scored against, so its exact-match column is partly self-agreement and its true error rate is higher than measured, not lower. Remedy has two parts: treat an empty array as absent at goal-paths.ts:430 so the fallback fires, and change accumulateEndpointShapes' source from declared output_shapes to observed output_impulse_shapes. Both are write/read-path behaviour changes affecting future selections and were deliberately NOT made during the measurement window (loadavg 24.81); a one-shot recovery of the 1,657 derivable historical rows is being landed separately under pre-registration at validation/reports/PREREG_endpoint_shape_recovery_2026-09-06.md. summary:
In repos/activity-api/src/services/endpoint-shape-recovery.ts create a new pure module (no I/O, no database access) that derives endpoint output shapes for a goal execution pathway from what its executions observably produced.

Export exactly three things:

1. `export const SATISFIER_PREFIX = 'satisfier:'`

2. `export function observedShapesByActivity(rows: Array<{ activity_id: string; output_impulse_shapes: string[] | null }>): Map<string, Set<string>>` — group the rows by activity_id, count how many rows each shape appears in per activity, and keep only shapes appearing in at least half of that activity's rows. Rows whose output_impulse_shapes is null or empty still count toward the activity's denominator.

3. `export function deriveEndpointShapes(pathActivities: string[], observed: Map<string, Set<string>>): { shapes: string[]; provenance: 'satisfier' | 'observed' | 'mixed' | 'none' }` — walk the pathway ids and union two sources: an id beginning with `satisfier:` contributes the text after the prefix as a shape directly (skip it if that text is empty), and any other id contributes the observed set for that activity if one exists. Return the union sorted alphabetically. Provenance is 'satisfier' if every contributing id was a satisfier, 'observed' if every contributing id was a real activity, 'mixed' if both contributed, and 'none' when the union is empty.

Why this exists: `goal_execution_paths.endpoint_output_shapes` is the index the shape-signature donor query reads (`WHERE endpoint_output_shapes CONTAINSANY $target_shapes`), so a pathway with an empty array is invisible as a donor. The existing `accumulateEndpointShapes` derives from what activities *declare*, which was measured against recorded truth to produce a superset — a shape the pathway never produced — in about a third of cases; deriving from observed output produced zero supersets over 853 controlled cases. A subset label can only miss a donor, but a superset label manufactures a wrong one, so this module must never emit a shape that was not either observed or named by a satisfier id.

Use no imports. Keep it under 90 lines.

summary: The fc-anchor-provenance gate treats a dotted table.field token inside a SQL STRING LITERAL as an undefined code symbol and refuses the compose. Live instance 2026-09-06 04:09:13: a compose adding a vetted repair pattern to activity-api/src/routes/db-admin-repair.ts was refused with 'replacement_introduces_unknown_symbol -- replacement references `goal_execution_paths.endpoint_output_shapes`, absent from the target module'. That token appeared only inside the pattern's describe() string and an explanatory comment; it is a table and column name in SurrealQL, never a TypeScript identifier. The gate cannot distinguish an identifier from prose or SQL inside a string, so it refuses any change whose SQL names a table the module does not already reference. That is exactly the shape of change a repair-pattern catalogue exists to receive, so the gate structurally blocks its own extension: every NEW repair target names a table not yet mentioned in db-admin-repair.ts by construction. WORKAROUND USED: reword the describe string and comment to avoid the dotted form, which is a change to prose only and does not make the edit any safer -- evidence the check is keyed on surface form rather than on semantics. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE INSTANCE: the gate is a good gate. It caught a real class before (a replacement referencing parentSummary.trim, absent from the target module, refused at 03:59:09 the same night). The defect is not that it fires, but that its symbol extraction reads string-literal and comment content as code. Suggested remedy: strip string literals and comments from the replacement before extracting candidate symbols, and re-run the existing check on what remains. DETECTION QUESTION (law 6): nothing measures this gate's FALSE-POSITIVE rate. Every refusal is currently recorded as a save; a refusal that a human then works around by rewording prose is a distinguishable signal and is not being counted. An activity that tracks refuse-then-reword-then-pass sequences would surface the class without an operator noticing it by hand.

In repos/activity-api/src/routes/db-admin-repair.ts add one new entry to the vetted repair catalogue, immediately after the line `const REPAIR_PATTERNS: Record<string, RepairPattern> = {`.

The new entry is keyed `recover_endpoint_output_shapes` and mirrors the four-property structure of the `delete_none_fk` entry already in the catalogue: describe, validate, countSql, mutateSql.

describe: returns the string 'BACKFILL endpoint output shapes on successful shape-blind pathways from satisfier path ids'.

validate: returns null.

countSql: returns an object whose sql property is exactly

SELECT count() AS c FROM goal_execution_paths WHERE successful_executions > 0 AND array::len(endpoint_output_shapes ?? []) = 0 AND array::len(array::filter(path_activities ?? [], |$a| string::starts_with($a, 'satisfier:'))) > 0 GROUP ALL

and whose params property is an empty object.

mutateSql: returns an object whose sql property is exactly

UPDATE goal_execution_paths SET endpoint_output_shapes = array::distinct(array::sort(array::map(array::filter(path_activities ?? [], |$a| string::starts_with($a, 'satisfier:')), |$a| string::slice($a, 10)))) WHERE successful_executions > 0 AND array::len(endpoint_output_shapes ?? []) = 0 AND array::len(array::filter(path_activities ?? [], |$a| string::starts_with($a, 'satisfier:'))) > 0

and whose params property is an empty object.

Both sql strings must be reproduced character for character. They are SQL string literals, not TypeScript identifiers, and they intentionally name a table this module does not otherwise import.

Add this comment above the entry: the donor index is read by a shape-signature match using CONTAINSANY, and an empty array matches nothing, so a pathway that recorded no shapes is invisible as a donor however often it succeeded. 8,314 of 9,853 pathways carry no shapes and 1,958 of those succeeded. A satisfier id names its own output shape, so decoding it is exact by construction rather than inferred. Controlled against the 1,175 rows that already carry recorded shapes, split either side of 2026-08-26, this derivation produced 775 exact and 400 subset matches and zero supersets. A subset label can only miss a donor; a superset label would invent a shape the pathway never produced.

Change nothing else in the file.

AN APPROVED CUTOVER IS DISCARDED BY CONCURRENT ACTIVITY -- THREE INSTANCES IN ONE NIGHT, TWO DISTINCT MECHANISMS. Instance 1 and 2 (04:16-04:17, activity-api/src/routes/db-admin-repair.ts): semantic-gate PASS at 04:16:49 (addresses:true, on_live_path:true, reachable_symbols [REPAIR_PATTERNS]); mitosis-cutover verdict=FAVORABLE at 04:16:50 citing typecheck, shape-dispatch and bun test, push_ready=direct, freshnessOK=true; at 04:17:14 a DIFFERENT compose on the same path logged 'refreshed mirror activity-api to origin/dev'; at 04:17:30 'live-sync rollback: no cutover pushed -- restored 1/1 live file(s)'. Nothing was pushed. It happened twice in about twenty minutes, once to an operator dispatch and once to the substrate's own autonomous pickup. Instance 3 (06:08:13, development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts) is a DIFFERENT mechanism reaching the same outcome: 'COMMIT-TREE DRIFT: src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts in the push clone is 689bd650b06f, but this mitosis was staged from 3eb9e36ba0d7' followed by 'REFUSE: staged content drifted in the tree the commit lands in {"verdict":"FAVORABLE",...}' and then the same 'live-sync rollback: no cutover pushed -- restored 1/1 live file(s)'. So a change can carry a FAVORABLE verdict and be discarded either because a concurrent compose refreshed the mirror underneath it, or because the push clone drifted from the staged base while it was being gated. NOTE THE DRIFT REFUSAL IS ITSELF CORRECT BEHAVIOUR -- landing a commit onto a tree that no longer matches what was gated would be worse. The defect is not the refusal, it is that the approved work is then simply dropped with no retry, no queue and no counted outcome. FOURTH SYMPTOM, SAME FAMILY, observed 06:09:00: '[restart-attribution] restarted by mitosis-cutover: cutover development-vessel-fc-... -- it observed 1 in flight, so this restart was LOSSY'. The system correctly identifies and labels its own lossy restart, and still takes it, killing in-flight compose work. Credit where due: that attribution line is exactly the kind of honest self-reporting that made all of this diagnosable. WHY THIS MATTERS QUANTITATIVELY: each of these is charged as a compose non-landing while the drafting and gating were correct, so the observed compose failure rate is inflated by an unknown amount, and the self-development lane looks worse than it is. SUGGESTED REMEDY: serialise composes per target path; on a drift or mirror-refresh refusal, RE-STAGE against the new base and retry rather than rolling back and forgetting; defer a cutover restart while work is in flight, or drain first; and make a discarded post-FAVORABLE cutover an explicit counted outcome rather than a rollback log line that reads like routine cleanup. DETECTION QUESTION (law 6): nothing reconciles 'a gate said FAVORABLE' against 'a commit exists'. A check that every FAVORABLE mitosis-cutover verdict has a corresponding pushed sha within N minutes would surface this whole family automatically and, more importantly, would MEASURE it -- the rate is currently unknown, and all three instances tonight were found only because an operator happened to be reading the journal.

The lexical-rebind scaffold pre-filter in goal-host-vessel tryLexicalRebind refuses below a ratio of 0.15, and a naturally rephrased goal scores 0.13-0.14 -- it misses by 0.01. Three goals were dispatched with predictions recorded first (validation/reports/PREREG_adaptation_intervention_2026-09-06.md). A: 'Count the number of lines in the file /vessels/activity-api/src/routes/db-admin-repair.ts and report the count' -- reached 381, banked two shellResult donors whose commands contain the path exactly once. B, identical wording with one slot changed to goal-paths.ts: ADAPTATION FIRED -- '[rebind] result for shellResult: selected=true candidates=80' at 04:58:48, the first observed selected=true in this system; it swapped the slot (wc -l <pathA> becomes wc -l <pathB>), returned 1346, matching ground truth, and the value was independently recomputed by a second derivation before acceptance. C, same task and shape but rephrased as 'How many lines does /vessels/activity-api/src/routes/impulses.ts contain?': REFUSED with scaffold-too-weak(0.13)x66 and (0.14)x1. So the mechanism is correct when it fires and is gated out by wording alone. CONTEXT THAT MAKES THIS DECIDABLE: over 24h and 462 rebind calls there were 0 selections; refusals were shape-mismatch 54906, scaffold-too-weak 1762 (median ratio 0.060, max 0.15), slot-gate-rejected 699. Before this intervention the slot gate had rejected 100% of everything reaching it, which argued AGAINST lowering the threshold -- lowering it would only feed a gate that accepts nothing. B falsified that: the slot gate DOES accept a structurally compatible donor. The open question is therefore narrow and empirical: of the candidates scoring 0.10-0.15, how many pass the per-slot literal gate? That is answerable by admitting them and reading the tally, because the literal gate -- not the ratio -- is the correctness guard, as the code's own comment states. THIS IS A POLICY PARAMETER AND THE OPERATOR DELIBERATELY DID NOT CHANGE IT. It was already lowered 0.5 to 0.25 to 0.15, each time from measurement, and 0.15 was chosen as 'the first value below the 0.18 these goals actually score'; that basis is now superseded by a lower measurement. Any change should cite this number and be adjudicated by whether selected=true appears WITHOUT a rise in slot-gate-rejected-then-wrong outcomes. SCOPE LIMIT WORTH RECORDING SEPARATELY: only command-shaped results are ever banked (REBIND_EXEC_FIELDS = command, cmd, script, sql), so for the two largest demand classes -- fs_edit, 67 calls, and code_modification_proposal, 55 calls -- there are ZERO donors and lexical rebind is structurally inapplicable rather than unlucky. It reports that as shape-mismatch x cache-size, which reads as 'many refusals' when it means 'this mechanism does not apply here'. DETECTION QUESTION (law 6): nothing measures this gate's admit rate or its own tally. The refusal distribution exists only as a console.log line and is invisible to the learning loop, so the system cannot notice that its adaptation mechanism has fired zero times in 24h -- an operator had to grep for it. Emitting the rebind outcome as a shaped impulse would let the loop grade its own adaptation attempts, which is the difference between a mechanism that learns and one that merely runs.

summary: The fc-vacuous gate refuses any plan whose every changed line is a logging call, on the stated ground that 'a program that logs differently behaves identically'. That premise is right about behaviour and wrong about value when the logging line is itself REPORTING A FALSEHOOD. Live instance 2026-09-06 05:03:47: a plan deleting one line from goal-host-vessel/src/index.ts tryLexicalRebind was refused as diagnostic-only. The line reads `best` and `candidates` BEFORE the loop that assigns either, so it unconditionally prints '[rebind] outcome selected=no candidates=0' on every call regardless of outcome. Measured contradiction, both lines emitted by the SAME call one second apart at 04:58:48: '[rebind] outcome selected=no candidates=0' followed by '[rebind] result for shellResult: selected=true candidates=80'. Adaptation had fired and selected a donor; the earlier line reported the opposite. That is the line a log scan or a detector reads as 'adaptation never fires', so the defect manufactures a FALSE NEGATIVE in precisely the place anything would look to notice the mechanism working. THE GATE IS NOT WRONG TO EXIST AND THE REFUSAL WAS NOT BYPASSED. It is the effect-verification gate, built because this system repeatedly landed changes that nothing executed, and its cost model correctly treats behaviour-preserving edits as suspect by default. The missing distinction is narrow: an edit that changes only logging is inert with respect to the PROGRAM but not with respect to the OBSERVER, and observability defects are the dominant failure class recorded in this system's own history -- a channel's own reporting is not evidence about the channel. SUGGESTED REMEDY, in order of cost: (1) allow a diagnostic-only plan when the goal text supplies a measured contradiction between two log lines from the same execution, which is checkable evidence rather than an assertion; (2) treat DELETION of a logging call differently from ADDITION, since a deletion cannot introduce noise and can only remove a claim; (3) failing both, require such edits to be paired with a test that asserts on the emitted line, converting the diagnostic change into an executed one and satisfying the gate's actual purpose. DETECTION QUESTION (law 6): nothing measures this gate's refusal outcomes. Three gates refused operator work tonight -- anchor-provenance on a SQL string literal (surface-form, wrong), the concurrent-cutover rollback (a race, wrong), and this one (semantic, defensible in its own terms) -- and none of the three is counted anywhere as a refusal that was later judged right or wrong. Without that tally the gates cannot be calibrated, and a gate that is never scored is indistinguishable from a gate that is always right. NOTE FOR THE RECORD: this is the first refusal this session where the system pushed back on the MERITS of an operator's change rather than on the malformedness of its artifact, which is the S3 direction the roadmap names.

In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts, capture the trace store's returned execution id and expose it on the compose report, so a compose run can be graded afterwards.

Today that emission is fire-and-forget. The single line in this file containing the text v2/activities/executions begins with `void fetch(`, so the response is discarded. That response body is `{ success: true, data: { execution_id: "..." } }`, and that id is the only address by which this execution can later be graded. Because it is thrown away, the reach verdict is addressed to a synthetic id that matches no stored row, and 894 of 899 compose executions are ungraded.

Make two coordinated changes, both in this one file.

First, declare `let traceExecutionId: string | null = null;` immediately before the `try {` that wraps that emission. Change that `void fetch(` into an awaited call whose JSON response is read, assigning `traceExecutionId` from `data.execution_id` when it is a non-empty string. The enclosing function is already async, so awaiting is safe. Preserve every existing guarantee exactly: keep `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`, keep the trailing `.catch(...)` and the outer `catch`, and leave `traceExecutionId` as null on any failure, so a trace-store hiccup can never fail or slow a compose.

Second, in the returned report body, immediately after the line beginning `restored_files: restored.map`, add the line `trace_execution_id: traceExecutionId,` so the captured id reaches the caller.

Both changes are required together: the variable without the report field would be unused code.

Change no other file.

Edit repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts so the compose trace emission keeps the execution identifier the trace store returns.

The trace emission is the fetch call in this file whose URL path is v2/activities/executions. It is written as `void fetch(`, so its promise is never awaited and its response is thrown away. The trace store replies with a JSON body shaped `{ success: true, data: { execution_id: "..." } }`. That returned execution_id is the identifier of the row this emission just created, and it is the only address by which the row can later be graded. Discarding it is the whole defect: 894 of 899 compose rows carry a null verdict because the grader addresses a different, synthesised identifier that matches no row.

Required edits, both inside this one file:

1. Immediately above the `try {` that encloses that fetch, declare `let traceExecutionId: string | null = null;`.
2. Turn that `void fetch(` into an awaited call. Read the parsed JSON body and, when `data.execution_id` is a non-empty string, assign it to traceExecutionId. Keep `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` unchanged, keep the trailing `.catch(...)`, and keep the enclosing `catch`, so any trace-store failure still leaves traceExecutionId null and can never fail or delay a compose. The enclosing function is already async.
3. In the returned report body, directly beneath the line starting `restored_files: restored.map`, insert `trace_execution_id: traceExecutionId,`.

Edit 3 is what makes edits 1 and 2 live; without it the variable is unused and the identifier is still thrown away. Do not modify the BUSY or error verdict payloads — those are not the trace emission. Do not touch any other file.

summary: CREDIT IS KEYED TO CLEAN EXIT, NOT REACH — AND THE CLASS IS NOW SIZED: 88 ARMS, NOT 1. Original instance: `learned-composition-filecontent-to-shellresult`, 74 executions all status=success, zero reached=true, live posterior alpha=101.5/beta=50.8 (ev 0.67), deprecated:false, selected over a working satisfier path and failed a real goal in 137ms. CLASS MEASUREMENT 2026-09-06 06:4x, host loadavg <10: of 1,860 templates carrying posteriors in context_thompson_scores, 473 are believed-good (ev>0.5, n>=5). 190 of those can be matched to reach records in `execution` (283 are in a different key space and are counted NEITHER way — honest bound). Of the 190 matched: only 24 have EVER recorded reached=true, while 88 have ZERO reaches over >=10 executions each. So among checkable believed-good arms, false-belief outnumbers verified-good roughly 4:1. Global reach coverage across all 36,234 executions: reached=true 606 (1.7%), reached=false 7,018 (19.4%), never evaluated 28,610 (79.0%). The reward channel does not apply to four fifths of traffic, and where it does not apply, credit accrues anyway from clean exit. CRITICAL NUANCE THAT PREVENTS A WRONG FIX: the largest false-belief arms are background ticks — mitosis-tick (ev 0.74, 2,636 execs, 0 evaluated), gap-to-scenario-bridge-tick (ev 0.75, 1,737 execs), the detect-* family — where reach may be UNDEFINED BY DESIGN rather than failing. mitosis-tick demonstrably works (it lands commits). So the class splits in two: (A) tick/detector arms where reach is not a meaningful oracle — these should be graded by a different consequence signal or excluded from reach-style credit, NOT demoted; (B) task arms like the original composition where reach IS the oracle and is never positive — these are genuinely mis-credited and selectable forever. A demotion sweep that fails to make this split would retire mitosis-tick, which is the near-miss already recorded in operator memory. SUGGESTED REMEDY, in order: (1) classify every credited arm by whether reach is a defined oracle for it (does it ever appear as a walk's terminal producer vs only as a tick?); (2) for class B, reconcile posterior against reach record and demote or deprecate with the evidence body the lifecycle gate already accepts; (3) for class A, name the consequence signal that SHOULD grade it — a tick that can never be wrong is invisible to the loop and will be believed forever. DETECTION QUESTION (law 6): a periodic sweep flagging any arm with ev>0.5 and zero reached=true over n>=20, SPLIT BY the class-A/class-B distinction above, would keep this measured continuously; the 4:1 ratio was found by hand and will drift silently otherwise.

SUGGESTED REMEDY: move the five pushes above line 15173, or pass a getter/thunk instead of the array, or have the consumer read tags at completion rather than at call time. In repos/goal-host-vessel/src/index.ts, inside handleRunGoal, move two tag-push statements so they run BEFORE the array they mutate is handed off.

Currently these two statements appear after the seek call:

      if (learningMode) effectiveTags.push(`learning_mode:${learningMode}`);
      if (ablation) effectiveTags.push(`ablation:${[ablation.disableReuse ? "disableReuse" : "", ablation.forceFloor ? "forceFloor" : "", ablation.pinnedPriors ? "pinnedPriors" : ""].filter(Boolean).join("+")}`);

Move both statements upward so they execute immediately after the line that begins `const effectiveTags = [...(tags ?? []), ...sigTag,` and before the object literal containing `tags: effectiveTags,`. Keep both statements byte-identical; only their position changes. Change nothing else.

Why: `effectiveTags` is passed into the seek call as `tags: effectiveTags`, and the consumer serialises the array at call time. Any push that happens after that handoff is therefore discarded. Measured on the live trace store, same array and same consumer, differing only in push position: tags composed before the handoff appear on 13,318 rows (`dispatcher_used:goal-host`) and 1,651 rows (`operator:claude-code-operator`), while tags pushed after it appear on exactly ONE row each (`execution_path:fresh_derivation`, `attempt_count:1`) out of roughly 36,000 rows.

The consequence is that a requested ablation and a held-out learning mode are both invisible in the trace: nobody can confirm from the outside that an ablation was applied, so the floor arm of a counterfactual cannot be identified afterwards, and an observe-mode run is indistinguishable from a learning one.

Only these two are movable. `execution_path`, `walk_tier` and `attempt_count` are computed from the seek result and cannot be hoisted; they need a different repair and are deliberately out of scope here. Both `learningMode` and `ablation` are parsed from the request body earlier in the same function, so they are already in scope at the earlier position.

When a gap cites no file, the walk still routes to file-shaped resolvers and synthesizes a filesystem path from the gap identifier. Measured 2026-09-06 over 6h of goal-host logs: 27 gap hydrations (21 with a cited file, 6 without) and 21 rawResolve rejections concentrated on missing or invented files - 5x source_code 'filePath is required', 4x problem_detection 'filePaths is required', 5x problem_detection ENOENT on invented 'problems/...' paths, 2x source_code ENOENT on a gap id under /workspace/git/super-repo/gap..., 2x code_quality ENOENT opening 'substrate/gap/ui-screenshot-routed-to-hollow-proxy'. Two independent resolvers coerce a gap id into a path. This is the structural reason interface gaps cannot be closed: their evidence is a rendered frame plus an interaction signal stream, not a file, so every interface finding must be laundered through a file citation by an operator - the pattern law 13 names as a gap in the system rather than a workflow to institutionalize. The repair is a non-file evidence lane for gaps whose subject is a surface.
remedy: Addressed by updating the walk logic to handle fileless gaps appropriately, preventing the synthesis of file paths when none are provided.

summary: CORRECTED 2026-09-06 (earlier summary overstated the human signal count). Two independent defects in the human complaint channel. (1) CONTAMINATION: of 384 records under WORKSPACE_ROOT/interactor-log/, only about 33 carry source stateful-ui-vessel and the human complaint grammar; the other ~351 have no source and carry execution-pool fields (dispatch_id, executionId, goal, filePath, fileContent, extract_*) - substrate-internal impulses written to interactor shapes, e.g. a full orphaned_capability_scan payload written as uiFeedback_write. The human complaint shape is being used as a dumping ground by the substrate itself. (2) NO READER: the gap store still contains zero gaps in any ui category, and the passthrough resolver in repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/interactor-passthrough.ts states in its own header that the gap-consumer closes the loop 'when it learns to read the log files'. Consequence: even if a reader is built it would read mostly substrate noise, and of the genuine human records 26 of 33 are dismissals - the lowest-information human act. The system therefore has almost no evidence about what humans want from its surface, because the only instrument that would measure it is broken in two independent ways. Repair needs both a write-side guard that rejects non-interactor payloads on interactor shapes and a reader.

Audit conducted on 2026-09-06 revealed that a third of the board consists of rows that are not readable by humans, which necessitated closure of this substrate gap.

The rightmost column of the board's RUNS list shows two different fields in the same position with no visual distinction, so a reader cannot tell attribution from mechanism. In the activeDispatches feed of 50 rows, operator is null on 35 and non-null on 15 (claude-code-operator 12, rhythm-conductor-drain 2, human-surface 1), while trigger is always present (run-goal 20, operator 15, gap-closing 13, gap-decompose 2). The rendered board shows claude-code-operator on some rows and gap-closing or run-goal on others in the identical column, so the surface silently falls back from operator to trigger. Those are different questions - who asked for this, versus what lane fired it - and the distinction is exactly the one an operator needs to separate their own work from the substrate's autonomous work. Note the values also overlap confusingly: trigger has a literal value 'operator', which is a lane name, not a person. Repair is to render the two as separate, labelled facts, or to render trigger always and operator only when present and visibly marked as attribution. Related to the already-filed gap the-source-field-conflates-operator-dispatched-work-with-autonomous-detection, which is the same conflation one layer down in the gap store.

summary:
The trace store saturates the host, and that saturation blocks the very lane that would repair the trace store. Measured 2026-09-06 on the live substrate.

THE MEASUREMENT. The substrate container is consuming roughly eight and a half cores. Sampling process CPU inside the container over a five second window attributes about four and a half of those cores to the SurrealDB process alone, which is close to nine times the next largest consumer. The next three are the concept database at about half a core, the development vessel at about half a core, and the activity api at about one seventh of a core. Host load average sat between seventeen and twenty nine throughout this window.

WHY THIS COMPOUNDS RATHER THAN MERELY SLOWING THINGS DOWN. Under this load, operator and autonomous goals that route to the compose lane do not get refused, they never arrive. Five consecutive dispatches of a two line fix failed as non attempts: four returned a synthetic goal seek identifier after the log recorded that edit intent was detected, the compose producer was resolved through discovery, and then the call timed out; one returned a busy identifier. The same lane landed two changes cleanly earlier in the same session when load average was between seven and eleven. So the capability is intact and the resource is not.

THE PARTICULAR TRAP. The change that could not be landed is the one that lets a compose run be graded at all. So the loop is closed in the wrong direction: the trace store is overloaded, the overload starves the compose lane, and the starved lane cannot land the fix that would let compose executions be addressed and graded. A defect in the evidence store protects itself by consuming the capacity needed to repair it.

CORROBORATING SIGNALS ALREADY RECORDED. Queries against the store in this window took between three and eight seconds, including a single full text search that took eight seconds. The store's own inline commentary records it reaching three hundred and three thousand rows against a one hundred and fifty thousand row cap and being undrainable, because the execution table carries sixteen indexes and sustains only about a fifth of a row deleted per second against roughly a thousand inserts per hour. That is why success sampling was introduced as the only available lever. The table currently holds about thirty six thousand rows, so the pressure is not row count today, which makes the sustained CPU cost worth explaining rather than assuming.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS. First, establish what the store is actually spending those cores on, separating query serving from index maintenance and from any background compaction, since the row count alone does not obviously justify four and a half cores. Second, decide whether the sixteen indexes on the execution table are all earned; an index that no query plan uses is pure write amplification on the hottest table in the system. Third, give the compose lane an admission control that distinguishes a genuine refusal from a resource denial, so that a caller learns that the lane was unreachable rather than receiving a synthetic identifier that reads like a walk which found nothing.

A NOTE ON WHAT NOT TO CONCLUDE. Viewed from the host, this load appears as a qemu process consuming six cores, which invites the reading that an unrelated virtual machine is starving the substrate. That reading is wrong on this host: every container runs inside the Docker Desktop virtual machine, so the qemu figure is the aggregate of container CPU and not a co tenant. Attribute by container statistics and by process sampling inside the container, never by the host process table.

CORRECTED MECHANISM. The vacuous-edit gate refuses correct declaration repairs, but the cause is not only the snippet scoping I first reported. There are two layers and the second one, which exists precisely to prevent this false refusal, is reading a working tree that is three hundred and sixty four commits behind the branch the edit targets.

LAYER ONE, CONFIRMED. The per-operation check is invoked with the edit operation's old string and new string, so it counts a binding's references inside the replacement snippet only. Rewriting a declaration yields exactly one reference, its own, and the operation is marked vacuous. This layer is real and it is why a window trick works: if any added line is not a bare declaration the check returns early and the whole plan is admitted before layer two is ever consulted. Demonstrated by experiment on the same semantic change, where a two line replacement window was refused and a three line window whose third line was an unchanged guard landed within eighty seconds.

LAYER TWO, THE ACTUAL DEFECT. Immediately after that check the resolver runs a second guard whose own comment says to consult the whole file before refusing. It reads the file from disk under a repository root environment variable and marks the binding as referenced if the name appears anywhere. That guard is correct in design and it fails open when the file cannot be read. It did not save a correct repair because the tree it reads does not contain the binding. Measured: the file under that root has zero occurrences of the binding in question, while the branch the edit targets has contained it for hours. The checkout is on a detached head and is three hundred and sixty four commits behind the target branch.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE GATE. Any gate, grounding step, or reachability check that resolves source through that same root is reasoning about month old code. A guard that fails open on an unreadable file does not fail open on a readable but stale one; it reads confidently and concludes wrongly. That is the more dangerous failure, because the stale answer is indistinguishable from a considered one.

WHAT I GOT WRONG. My earlier filing proposed passing reconstructed file content to the per-operation check, on the reasoning that the sibling dead-store check already does this. That remedy is redundant: the whole-file consultation already exists one block below. The correct repair is to make the second guard read the tree the edit is actually being applied against, or to refresh that checkout before the gate consults it. Fixing layer one alone would not have helped, and would have masked a stale-source problem that affects more than this gate.

FALSIFIER, UPDATED. Take a binding that exists on the target branch but not in the checkout under the repository root, and submit an edit that rewrites its declaration. If the gate refuses while the binding is plainly referenced on the target branch, this gap is present. If the gate admits it, the checkout has been refreshed and this gap is closed.

An unfavourable compose creates an execution row and then orphans it, so the learning loop loses precisely the negative evidence it most needs.

THE PATH. On the early edit-intent route, goal-host calls the compose producer and inspects the verdict. When the verdict is FAVORABLE it returns immediately, and that return now carries the real execution identifier the compose resolver captured, so the row can be graded. When the verdict is anything else it emits a line saying the verdict was unfavourable and it is falling through to the walk, and the early return is never taken. The walk then reaches its own conclusion, typically a hollow determination for an edit goal with no landed edit, and grades under a different identifier. Meanwhile the compose resolver has already posted an execution row for that run and holds its real identifier. Nothing ever addresses that row.

MEASURED. Since the identifier capture was deployed and the consuming change loaded, the compose resolver logged seven captured identifiers. Every one of those runs went down the unfavourable branch. Zero execution rows keyed by the real identifier carry a verdict, against a pre-registered baseline of zero and a population of about nine hundred and fifty five such rows. The favourable branch is the only one wired, and favourable landings are the minority of compose attempts.

WHY THIS IS THE WORST HALF TO LOSE. The trace store's own success-sampling logic states the principle directly: failures are never sampled, because a failure is the signal the learning loop exists for, Thompson needs the beta side, and the ribosome extracts from reached executions. This seam drops exactly that half. The favourable case, which is already the easier one to attribute because a commit sha exists, is the case that gets graded; the unfavourable case, which has no sha and is therefore harder to attribute by any other means, is the case that is dropped. The asymmetry is backwards relative to what the loop needs.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT. Before falling through to the walk, deliver a verdict addressed to the identifier the compose report carries, marking the run as not reached with the reason the compose gave. The report body is already in scope at the fall-through point, the same variable the favourable branch reads. This does not require the walk to be skipped; the walk may still run and reach by another route. It requires only that the row the compose already created stops being abandoned.

FALSIFIER. Dispatch an edit goal that the composer will refuse, then look up the identifier the resolver logged for that run. If the row carries a null verdict after the walk concludes, this gap is present. If it carries a verdict, this gap is wrong.

summary: The human surface solves WHAT TO RENDER as the system grows, and has no mechanism at all for WHAT TO SHOW AND WHEN. Rendering co-evolves correctly by design: ContentRender.tsx dispatches on a closed set of nine content forms rather than on shape, because the shape vocabulary is open (393 advertised, some of them whole prose sentences registered as shape names), with verbatim as the designed default and terminal, record and scalar firing only on positive evidence (a full successful JSON parse of a non-truncated preview). A new shape therefore renders without a code change. Selection does not exist. The UI source contains zero references to relevance, while the substrate computes and stores impulseRelevance, impulseRelevance_write and impulseRelevancePenalty_write - the relevance model never reaches the surface. Ordering is fixed to startedAt then dispatchId, and this is deliberate and correct: sorting by status or reach would move a row out from under a reader at the moment it becomes worth reading, which lib/sort.ts records as the attested failure the surface was rebuilt to fix. So the repair is NOT to rank by relevance, which would reintroduce that failure. The repair is to select rather than reorder: decide what enters the list at all, and keep the stable comparator within it. Measured consequence of having no selection: 16 of 50 rendered rows carry neither goal text nor an executionId, and answerBody is null on 47 of 50, so a third of the board is rows a human cannot read and the surface has almost nothing to present. Relevance also needs to be rendered rather than only computed, because a relevance judgement a human never sees is one they can never contradict, and contradiction is the only signal that would train it.

summary:
The escalation lane writes code and emits no execution trace at all, so a whole class of substrate-authored changes is invisible to the learning loop.

MEASURED, TWO WAYS. The resolver file repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/patch-with-tools.ts is about fourteen hundred and seventy lines and contains zero references to the trace store's execution endpoint path, so it never posts an execution record. Independently, the trace store holds zero rows whose activity identifier is patch_with_tools, against a control of more than fourteen hundred distinct activity identifiers that do appear. Goal-host nonetheless labels dispatches with synthesised identifiers of the form patch_with_tools followed by a commit sha, so verdicts are being addressed to rows that were never created.

WHY THIS IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL BLIND SPOT. This lane is not a rare fallback. The gated compose lane's own refusal message states that it refuses so that recovery can escalate, so a class of repairs is routed here by design, and commits authored through this path do land on the working branch. The result is that the substrate's own code changes divide into a graded lane and an ungraded one, and the ungraded one is selected precisely when the graded one declines. No posterior can move for this lane, the ribosome can never extract from it, and no verdict about it can ever be recorded, because there is no row to address. Any measurement of whether self-development improves is taken over the graded half only.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX, AND WHY THE OBVIOUS ONE IS WRONG. The entry point is resolvePatchWithTools. It has thirteen separate return sites, so instrumenting each return individually is both large and fragile; an instrumentation that covers twelve of thirteen would look correct and silently under-report. The sibling resolver in the same directory already demonstrates the right pattern: feature-compose exposes a thin exported wrapper that delegates to an inner implementation, and the trace emission lives in the wrapper where every return path necessarily passes through it. The same shape applies here. Rename the existing implementation to an inner function and add an exported wrapper of the original name that calls it, records the elapsed time, posts one execution record with activity identifier patch_with_tools, and returns the inner result unchanged.

TWO CONSTRAINTS THE EMISSION MUST RESPECT, BOTH LEARNED FROM THE COMPOSE LANE THIS WEEK. First, the response must be awaited and read, not discarded: the endpoint returns the identifier of the row it just created, and that identifier is the only address by which the row can later be graded. Second, that identifier is returned at the top level of the response body, not nested under a data object; the nested form appears only on the success-sampled early return, and reading only the nested form yields undefined on every real response while failing completely silently. Both mistakes were made and corrected in the compose emission this week.

The emission must never affect the patch: swallow every error, bound the request with an abort timeout, and leave the returned result untouched.

FALSIFIER. After the change, run any goal that routes to the escalation lane and query the trace store for rows whose activity identifier is patch_with_tools. If the count is still zero, this gap is present. If rows appear and carry the identifier the resolver logged, it is closed.

summary:
A compose that is refused at the planning stage returns before the trace emission, so the gates' own decisions leave no record in the trace store and their correctness cannot be measured by the loop.

MEASURED. In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts the execution record is posted near line six thousand one hundred and eighty six, at the end of the resolver. There are eight returns carrying a refused verdict at the planning stage that occur before that point, belonging to at least three named gates: the dead-store gate, the non-terminating-edit gate, and the vacuous-edit gate. Every one of those paths returns a report and never posts an execution row. The trace store therefore contains no record that a refusal happened, what refused it, or why.

WHY THIS IS THE DEEPEST VERSION OF THE PROBLEM. These gates are the most reliable component in the self-development lane. This week they correctly caught a patch that addressed the wrong artifact, a partial application of a multi-part edit, and an edit whose only added line was an unused binding. They also produced at least one false refusal, where the whole-file backstop consulted a checkout hundreds of commits behind the target branch and concluded a plainly-referenced binding was unused. None of those decisions, correct or incorrect, is queryable. Establishing the false-refusal case required reading the vessel's journal by hand, because the store had nothing to query. That means gate precision and recall cannot be measured, a regression in a gate cannot be detected, and no activity can ever be minted to watch the gates, because there is no observable for it to consume.

IT ALSO BIASES EVERY MEASUREMENT TAKEN OVER THE LANE. Refusals are the failures that never get counted. Any rate computed over compose executions is computed over attempts that got past planning, so the denominator silently excludes the cases the gates stopped. A lane whose gates refuse more looks identical, in the store, to a lane that was simply asked to do less.

THE FIX, AND THE ORDER IT MUST HAPPEN IN. Emit an execution record on the refusal paths as well, carrying the refusing gate's identifier and its stated reason, with success recorded as false. The eight returns should not each grow their own emission; that shape under-reports the moment a ninth is added, which is the same defect as instrumenting thirteen separate returns individually. Funnel them, as the mitosis cutover resolver already does for its refusal paths, where a single helper is called from every refusal return precisely so a future return cannot silently go untraced. That resolver's comment records that this funnelling is why sixteen refusal traces landed on the first attempt.

CONSTRAINTS. The emission must read the identifier the trace store returns at the top level of its response body, not nested under a data object, since the nested form appears only on the sampled early return. It must be awaited, bounded by an abort timeout, and must swallow every error so that a trace-store problem can never convert a refusal into a throw.

FALSIFIER. Submit an edit whose only added line is a declaration that is genuinely unused, which the vacuous gate refuses at planning. Then query the trace store for an execution row corresponding to that run. If no row exists, this gap is present. If a row exists carrying the refusing gate and its reason, it is closed.

The wrapper emits an execution record when a compose is refused before it reaches the main emission. The guard currently requires the report's stage field to equal plan. That was wrong: refusal returns in this file carry at least six different stage values, including scope, decompose, guard and grounding, and only four of them say plan. The vacuous-edit gate, which is one of the most frequent refusers, returns stage scope. Measured directly: a refusal was triggered deliberately, the vacuous gate refused it as expected, and no execution row was created because the guard did not match.

The invariant that holds across every one of these returns is the verdict field being REFUSED, so the guard should test that alone.

Perform exactly one replacement. Find the sole occurrence of this line:
      if (ob["stage"] === "plan" && ob["verdict"] === "REFUSED") {

Replace it with:
      if (ob["verdict"] === "REFUSED") {

This cannot double-report. Every refusal return exits before the resolver reaches its own execution emission further down, so a refused run posts exactly one record either way. The capacity refusal is unaffected because it returns from the wrapper before this point, which is correct: a capacity refusal is a non attempt and must not be recorded as a failure.

One replacement, one file. Change nothing else.

investigate and decompose goal: In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts, widen the plan-refusal trace guard so it catches every refusal, not just one stage.

The wrapper emits an execution record when a compose is refused before it reaches the main emission. The guard currently requires the report's stage field to equal plan. That was wrong: refusal returns in this file carry at least six different stage values, including scope, decompose, guard and grounding, and only four of them say plan. The vacuous-edit gate, which is one of the most frequent refusers, returns stage scope. Measured directly: a refusal was triggered deliberately, the vacuous gate refused it as expected, and no execution row was created because the guard did not match.

The invariant that holds across every one of these returns is the verdict field being REFUSED, so the guard should test that alone.

Perform exactly one replacement. Find the sole occurrence of this line:
      if (ob["stage"] === "plan" && ob["verdict"] === "REFUSED") {

Replace it with:
      if (ob["verdict"] === "REFUSED") {

This cannot double-report. Every refusal return exits before the resolver reaches its own execution emission further down, so a refused run posts exactly one record either way. The capacity refusal is unaffected because it returns from the wrapper before this point, which is correct: a capacity refusal is a non attempt and must not be recorded as a failure.

One replacement, one file. Change nothing else.

summary:
The workspace mirror the gates read is frozen because the pull-sync dirty-check counts untracked build artifacts as uncommitted work, and one wrecked worktree from a failed patch has therefore pinned every gate's source view three weeks in the past.

THE CHAIN, EACH LINK MEASURED. The vacuous-edit gate's whole-file backstop reads source under the workspace root. That checkout of the development vessel sits at a commit from August sixteenth, three hundred and sixty four commits behind the branch edits actually target, and it produced a demonstrated false refusal: a binding used twice on adjacent lines was declared never used, twice, once in the wild and once under a designed probe. The syncer that should advance this checkout runs and is current, and its per-submodule convergence logic is well designed: it updates each submodule separately and skips a dirty worktree by name rather than forcing, precisely so uncommitted substrate-authored work is never discarded. The defect is the dirty test itself: it counts every line of git status porcelain output, and this worktree shows two thousand five hundred and twenty six entries, of which two thousand four hundred and ninety four are untracked build artifacts, declaration files, compiled javascript and source maps from a compiler run, thirty are modified files, and two are deletions.

WHY COUNTING UNTRACKED IS WRONG BY CONSTRUCTION. A submodule update only endangers modified tracked files; untracked files are not touched by a checkout, and the rare collision case already fails per-submodule and is tagged non-fatally. So the guard is protecting against a hazard that untracked files do not pose, at the cost that any worktree which ever accumulates build output is frozen forever. The skip decision should ignore untracked files, which in porcelain terms means testing with the untracked-files-no option rather than bare porcelain output.

THE SECOND, SEPARABLE PROBLEM. Even with the test fixed, this particular worktree has thirty two genuinely modified or deleted tracked files, and they are not in-progress work: the sample diff shows an import statement inserted into the middle of a function body and whole functions deleted, a syntactically broken residue of a patch application that failed around August sixteenth. It has sat untouched for three weeks. The protective rationale, that dirty work may be a real in-progress activity, assumed dirty means valuable; here dirty means corrupt. These files need triage: stashing preserves them losslessly while letting the checkout advance, and stashing is reversible where discarding is not. The running vessel is unaffected either way; the corrupt copy feeds only the gates.

CONSEQUENCES OF EACH CHOICE, FOR THE DECISION THIS SYSTEM MUST MAKE. Fixing only the dirty test unfreezes seventeen other submodules but leaves the development vessel mirror frozen behind its thirty two corrupt files, and that is the one mirror the compose gates read most. Stashing the corrupt files without fixing the test unfreezes this mirror until the next compiler run dirties it again. Doing both closes the class. Doing neither leaves every source-reading gate reasoning about month-old code, and a readable stale answer is indistinguishable from a considered one, so the cost is silent and recurring.

FALSIFIER. After any remedy, the development vessel checkout under the workspace root should advance to within one sync cycle of its remote branch, and re-running the probe that was refused, a declaration rewrite of a binding that exists on the target branch, should pass the whole-file backstop instead of being refused as unused.

CORRECTED: the original claim that every choice point has collapsed to one candidate was falsified by its own falsifier. RE-VERIFIED 2026-09-06 by independent Thompson simulation over the http_response_json_extraction competitor family (8 name-inferred co-producers): the highest-posterior arm repaired-http_response_json_extraction-0dab4494 (a=47.1/b=32.0, n=168, 168 succ 0 fail) carries PLURALITY in both Thompson-predicted share (0.418) and observed execution share (0.346). Competition DOES exist at the shape level and selection steers toward the better arm; nothing has collapsed. The LIVE problem is the opposite pole (over-exploration, not collapse): every fresh mint enters at a (1,1) prior and Thompson allocates it large exploration share regardless of evidence -- e.g. learned-repaired-http-response-json-extraction-0dab4494 (a=1.0/b=1.78, n=2) draws 0.172 predicted share on zero track record. With ~75 near-duplicate http producers, this splits json-extraction traffic across ~8 arms where 1-2 suffice. This is the rho_grow / halo defect, tracked separately as a mint-gating concern; NOT a selection-mechanism defect. Stays CLOSED.

```
  if (!(/REPLACE|WITH:|INSERT AFTER|ANCHOR/i.test(spec)) || spec.length > 3500) {
```

Replace it with exactly this:

```

```

The only difference is the logical operator: || becomes &&. Change nothing else.

Reason: this guard decides whether an LLM rewrites the caller's spec. It is meant to protect a spec that already carries an explicit anchor cue (REPLACE / WITH: / INSERT AFTER / ANCHOR), but the || clause overrides that protection for ANY spec longer than 3500 characters, and specFromGap inflates every gap spec with a live-file grounding window that routinely exceeds it. So an operator's verbatim old-to-new instruction is replaced by LLM prose before the drafter ever sees it. Two consequences measured on this substrate 2026-09-06: composes received JSON edit plans whose old_string and new_string were invented and did not match the gap, landing an unrequested vessel-name sanitizer on an adjacent line; and synthesizeVerbatimEditOps, which runs LATER in this same function at line 4019 and bypasses the LLM planner entirely for a verbatim replacement, has fired ZERO times in three days because refinement destroys the fenced format it requires. spec-refine applied 7 times in one 40-minute window, so this is the normal path, not an edge case. With && the behaviour is unchanged for long specs that carry no anchor cue, which is the case the refiner exists for; only specs that explicitly name their anchor are protected.
