summary: The dominant compose apply-failure mode is a NON-UNIQUE planned anchor, not a missing one. Measured: a plan for repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts used old_string `return null;`, which occurs 41 times in that file. feature-compose then correctly FAILS CLOSED - anchorRejected = anchorNonUnique && !groundedPre causes it to skip fs_edit entirely rather than mislocalize onto the first of many occurrences - so ops_applied is 0 and the compose fails. Critically the blind-edit anchor repair is ALSO skipped on this path, because its guard excludes anchorRejected. So the repair only ever addresses ABSENT anchors while the common failure is AMBIGUOUS ones. In the same trace the system had already logged `[fc-anchors] supplied verified-unique anchors for ... (57 locator candidate(s))` - it computes anchors verified to occur exactly once and the drafter did not use one. PROPOSED CHANGE: at plan time, before attempting fs_edit, check that each planned old_string occurs exactly once in the target file; when it does not, substitute the supplied verified-unique locator candidate that encloses or is nearest the intended statement, and only fail closed if no such candidate exists. safeAnchorLines() already computes that list with an exactly-once guarantee, so this reuses existing machinery.

classification_metadata.evidence: Measured 2026-09-09. DIRECT OBSERVATION: at 12:35 the fc-plan for feature-compose.ts logged ops [{kind:edit, old:"return null;"}]; grep -c of that string in the deployed file returns 41. summary: The failure-lesson diagnostic filter in feature-compose.ts selects stored lines with /error TS\d+|\berror\b|\d+ fail|FAIL|Error:/i. Because the regex is case-insensitive, the FAIL alternative matches PASSING test lines whose NAME contains the word fails - e.g. '(pass) both gates FAIL OPEN - a check that cannot decide must allow'. When such lines exist diagLines is non-empty, so the code stores them and DISCARDS the real compiler error. Observed on gap route-edit-7f78e742, whose stored lesson is entirely passing test output with zero lines matching an actual error. FIXED by commit be5298c which excludes lines whose trimmed form starts with (pass); this gap is retained as the record of the defect class since the fix itself was a repair of an earlier fix (f57d08b) that had introduced it.

summary:
CORRECTED 2026-09-10. My first filing of this gap said the signed-trace revert was inert and that the defect lay in the trace sender or its receiver. That diagnosis was WRONG, and the correction matters more than the original claim.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. The revert is landed and deployed; the running goal-host builds the trace id in the correct namespace. No signed row appears because NOTHING LANDS. A rich trace is only written on the branch taken after a compose returns a landed sha, and no edit-intent compose has produced one since the restart. The sink is not failing: its failure path logs a named message on every error and that message occurs ZERO times in the window. It is never reached.

THE REAL CONSTRAINT, measured from the goal-host journal by day. Favorable versus unfavorable edit-intent compose verdicts: Sep 07, 5 against 137, a 4 percent pass rate. Sep 08, 2 against 140, 1 percent. Sep 09, 3 against 119, 2 percent. Sep 10, 0 against 19, 0 percent. The semantic gate has been refusing between 96 and 99 percent of edit-intent composes for at least four days.

THE CONTROL THAT PREVENTED AN OVERCLAIM. Todays zero-of-nineteen looks like a total failure but is entirely consistent with the four-day baseline; at a 2 percent pass rate, seeing no pass in nineteen attempts is the ordinary outcome. This is NOT a new regression. Reporting it as one would have been wrong, and the multi-day denominator is what showed that.

WHY THIS IS THE BINDING ITEM. The action-to-verdict-to-belief seam cannot be exercised while almost nothing reaches the landing branch. Every downstream mechanism that depends on a landed change - the signature, the derived state signature, the credit that follows it - is starved upstream rather than broken. A fix aimed at the trace path cannot be validated until something lands.

RELATED AND LOAD-BEARING. On 2026-09-06 this same gate refused a fix that was demonstrably correct, agreeing two of two adversarial refuters at confidence 1.00, and citing two counter-examples that the rejected change provably handles. One proven-false refusal does not establish the false-refusal RATE, but it does mean the 96 to 99 percent refusal rate cannot be assumed correct, and the rate is measurable: for any refusal whose stated reason contains a concrete literal input, evaluate that literal against the changed predicate. That check is filed separately.

FALSIFIER. Two measurements, both currently failing. First: count edit-intent composes returning a favorable verdict per day; this is currently between 0 and 5 against roughly 130 attempts. Second: count execution rows whose id lies in the feature_compose namespace and whose signature is non-empty, in a window after a goal-host restart; this is currently zero, and cannot become non-zero until the first measurement does.

A DENOMINATOR WARNING FOR ANYONE QUOTING THIS. There are roughly 12,500 execution rows stamped with this activity id since the restart, but they are NOT composes. Sampled rows carry 15 to 18 fields, durations near 300 milliseconds, zero tokens and no status, against 26 fields and a populated signature on a genuine pre-2026-09-06 compose row. Field-key count is the writer fingerprint. Do not use that row count as a denominator for compose attempts; use the journal verdict counts.

summary: When two composes touch the same file, a failing attempt's rollback can revert a DIFFERENT attempt's already-successful change. The rollback restores preEditContent, a snapshot each compose takes on first touch of a file. If compose B starts before compose A's write lands, B's snapshot predates A's change, so B's rollback writes the pre-A content back and silently destroys A's landed work. MAX_CONCURRENT_COMPOSES is 4 and the composeInFlight guard only serialises UNISOLATED vessels, so two composes on the same file can overlap. OBSERVED TWICE on 2026-09-09. Case 1: at 01:24:17 a compose on gap route-edit-cd20dbbc succeeded outright - verify_ok=[true], rolled_back=false, and the semantic gate approved it in as many words - and at 01:26:37 a second attempt on the SAME gap failed verify, rolled back, and the operator-verified change was gone from the deployed tree with no commit. Case 2: earlier the same day a patch_with_tools edit applied and reported verified-green terminal, and a concurrent feature_compose on the same file rolled back and reverted it. PROPOSED CHANGE: make the rollback conditional rather than blind. Before writing preEditContent back, read the file's current bytes; restore only if they still match what THIS compose left there, and when they do not, skip the restore and log the skip with the path, because a mismatch means another writer has touched the file and this compose no longer owns it. Alternatively serialise composes per FILE rather than per vessel, extending the existing composeInFlight guard from vessel keys to absolute paths.

classification_metadata.evidence: Measured 2026-09-09/10 on the live substrate. EXECUTION RECORDS for gap route-edit-cd20dbbc: 01:24:17 apply_failed=false ops_applied=1 rolled_back=FALSE verify_ok=[true], semantic_reason 'The patch prevents the store from overwriting valid data with an empty array on parse failures, thereby addressing the described gap'; 01:26:37 apply_failed=false ops_applied=1 rolled_back=TRUE verify_ok=[false]. After the second execution the deployed file no longer contained the change and git log -S with pathspec found no commit, so the successful change was reverted rather than merely uncommitted. The change was re-dispatched and then landed and committed as ac61fe4. MECHANISM IN CODE: preEditContent is populated with `if (!preEditContent.has(abs)) preEditContent.set(abs, cur)` on first touch; the rollback loop iterates `for (const [abs, original] of preEditContent)` and writes original back, verifying only that the write took effect (rollbackRestoreIsVerified compares the read-back to original) and never that restoring was SAFE. CONCURRENCY: MAX_CONCURRENT_COMPOSES = 4, and the composeInFlight guard filters to unisolated vessels only, so two composes on one file can overlap. RELATED PRIOR ART in the same file: the step-4 rollback comment records an earlier incident where a rollback left discovery-vessel/src/index.ts at 2,449 bytes against 23,746 in its clone.

Edit repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/rhythm-reality-sync.ts. One file.

This resolver reads an open-gap count and uses it to recompute the gap-closing rhythm staleness. Two linked defects make it permanently suppress that rhythm.

CHANGE 1 - the timeout is shorter than the call. The gap_lifecycle_scan resolve is given a 2000 ms budget. Measured just now against the live substrate on three consecutive runs it takes 3749, 5350 and 5132 ms, so the abort fires every time. Raise that 2000 to 15000. The literal to change is the line containing only:
      2000,
which is the second argument of the fetchWithTimeout call that posts the gap_lifecycle_scan impulse. Do not change any other timeout in the file.

CHANGE 2 - and this is the important one - the failure path coerces UNKNOWN into a MEANINGFUL value. This line occurs exactly once, indented with six spaces:
      openGapCount = typeof data?.body?.open === "number" ? data.body.open : 0;
On a timeout, a non-ok response, or a missing field, openGapCount becomes 0, and 0 does not mean unknown here - it means the backlog is empty. staleness is then computed as min(1, openGapCount / targetBacklog) = 0 and written back, marking the family whose job is draining gaps as having nothing to do. With 1038 gaps currently open the gap-closing rhythm can never become due.

Introduce a boolean, declared alongside the existing openGapCount declaration and initialised false, that records whether a real count was obtained. Set it true ONLY on the branch where the numeric field was actually present. Leave it false in the catch and on a non-ok response.

Then guard the recomputation: when that boolean is false, skip the staleness recomputation and the write-back entirely and leave the stored staleness untouched. Abstaining preserves the last known-good value; writing a fabricated zero destroys it. Report the abstention in the returned body by carrying the flag, so a caller can tell an abstention from a genuine zero backlog.

Do not change how staleness is computed when the count IS known, do not touch the other rhythm families, and edit no other file.

The learning-signal health observer reports success_credit_ratio 1.0 and diagnosis "healthy" while the true fleet ratio is 0.456 and the subgroup it exists to watch is 0-for-17. It has moved from honestly abstaining to actively asserting the opposite of the truth, which is worse than being disarmed.

MEASURED 2026-09-10. Resolving {type:"learning_signal_health_observer"} returns total_concepts 5000, loaded_concepts 5000, loaded_with_success 5000, success_credit_ratio 1, enough_volume true, diagnosis "healthy". The store at the same moment: 69,142 concepts, 36,530 with times_loaded>0, 16,673 of those with times_succeeded>0 — a true ratio of 0.456. For source_type='compose_lesson': 17 loaded, 0 ever succeeded.

ROOT CAUSE - THE SAMPLE IS SELECTED BY THE QUANTITY BEING MEASURED. The observer fetches /concepts/search with NO query, which takes concept-db's relevance DESC ordering branch, and relevance is (times_succeeded + 1) / (times_loaded + 2). Ordering by relevance therefore returns precisely the concepts that HAVE successes. total, loaded and loaded_with_success are all exactly 5000 because the numerator chose the denominator. CONFIRMED EXPERIMENTALLY: concept_mdEvyKBG2IIs (relevance 0.0023, 433 loads, 0 successes) is absent from the sample — running the observer does not touch it — because it sits at the bottom of the very ordering the sample uses.

A SYMPTOM-ONLY PATCH WAS CORRECTLY REFUSED. On 2026-09-10 an attempt added a sample-saturation guard so the observer would abstain when its page filled to the limit. All three edits applied cleanly, and the semantic gate refused it 2/2: "addresses the symptom but does not address the underlying gap. The core problem is that the /concepts/search endpoint is being called with no query." That verdict is correct and should be preserved: abstaining is more honest than a false all-clear, but it is not a fix. Do not resubmit a guard alone.

WHAT THE ENDPOINT ACTUALLY SUPPORTS - THIS IS THE MATERIAL THAT MAKES A REAL FIX POSSIBLE. concept-db's GET /concepts/search parses query, shape, source_type, min_relevance, limit AND offset (src/routes/concepts.ts). Two consequences: (1) a source_type filter returns a WHOLE SUBGROUP rather than the top of a global relevance-ordered list — compose_lesson is roughly 36 concepts, so a filtered query returns all of them and its ratio is exact, not sampled; (2) offset permits paging, so a population-wide figure can be accumulated rather than approximated by one biased page.

THE FIX HAS TWO HALVES AND NEITHER WORKS ALONE. (1) SAMPLING: stop deriving any verdict from a single unfiltered relevance-ordered page. Prefer per-source_type queries using the source_type filter, since each returns its whole subgroup. (2) SUBGROUPS: report a per-source_type breakdown rather than one fleet aggregate — even a CORRECT fleet ratio of 0.456 would mask compose_lesson at 0/17. Fixing sampling alone leaves the masking; fixing subgroups alone computes every subgroup from a biased page.

MIND THE VOLUME FLOOR WHEN ADDING SUBGROUPS. min_loaded_volume defaults to 50, which no individual subgroup may reach — compose_lesson has 17 loaded. A subgroup verdict needs its own smaller floor, or the breakdown will be computed and then suppressed, reproducing in the subgroup layer the exact "permanently cold start" defect this observer already had at fleet level.

NOT THE CAUSE - RULED OUT BY CONTROL, DO NOT PURSUE. It was hypothesised that the observer pollutes its own metric, because /concepts/search calls recordPassiveUsageForResults and passive-usage.ts states that without a usage row "times_loaded never increments". Tested twice: a low-relevance concept (concept_mdEvyKBG2IIs) and the highest-relevance loaded concept (concept_L3kuQMZNfuLM, 235 loads) both showed times_loaded UNCHANGED across an observer run. The REST search path does not increment loads for this caller. The conceptSearch RESOLVER path does — two probes through it moved concept_mdEvyKBG2IIs from 431 to 433 — so the drafter's own lesson recall records loads while this observer does not. Do not "fix" pollution here; it is not happening.

ALSO REMOVE THE DEAD DECLARATION. `const subgroupSuccessCreditRatios = {}; // to hold ratios per source_type` is declared, never populated and never read. It was landed by 80ff131 to satisfy a Class-1 predicate whose expected_literal was "source_type" — a literal that occurs in this file exactly once, inside that comment. It certified a change that did nothing and should not survive this fix.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY, NOT TEXTUALLY. Resolve {type:"learning_signal_health_observer"} and compare its reported success_credit_ratio against the store's own count of concepts with times_loaded>0 versus times_succeeded>0 (currently 0.456, reported as 1.0), and require a per-source_type breakdown that shows compose_lesson separately. No string in any file can satisfy that.

summary:
substrateGap_write returns {"success":false,"error":"Failed to trigger gap-compose for <id>. See logs for details."} when the gap write itself SUCCEEDED and only a post-write side effect stumbled. The caller is told its write failed when the row is in the store, correct and complete.

OBSERVED 2026-09-10 05:58:02, on a rewrite of gap `compose-lessons-are-loaded-but-never-credited-so-their-relevance-decays-with-use`. The resolver returned success:false. A read-back one second later showed the write had fully landed: the new 4,165-character summary was present and every metadata field was preserved (falsifier class1, edit_site, failed_attempts 2, failure_lessons).

THE TRIGGER DID NOT EVEN FAIL. The journal for that same second carries BOTH of these lines:

    [substrate-gap] gap-compose service start failed with exit code null
    [substrate-gap] event-driven gap-compose pickup triggered by <id> (service started successfully)

So a first start attempt returned a null exit code, a retry succeeded, and the resolver reported the FIRST outcome as the result of the whole operation. The compose ran.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. A write resolver that reports failure on success trains every caller to do the wrong thing. An operator or activity that believes the write failed will retry it, and substrateGap_write REPLACES rather than merges, so a retry built from a stale local copy silently reverts whatever the first write actually stored. This is the same class as the reach verdict being reported before the graded result is confirmed: the caller's view of what happened diverges from what happened, and the divergence is invisible unless someone reads the row back.

FIX. The return value must describe the WRITE. A failure to trigger a downstream compose is a separate, best-effort concern and belongs in a distinct field (for example trigger_status) or in the log alone, never in `success`. If the trigger genuinely matters to the caller, report it as its own outcome rather than overwriting the write's. While there, make the trigger report its FINAL state rather than its first attempt, since a retry that succeeds should not surface as a failure at all.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. Write a gap through substrateGap_write, read the same id back, and confirm that a response carrying success:false never coexists with a stored row matching what was sent. No string in any file establishes that.

summary:
The rhythm registry was restored on 2026-09-10 and the conductor reads all eleven families, yet nothing is ever enqueued. The cause is not the registry and not the conductor: ten of the eleven families have no mechanism by which their staleness can ever rise, so they can never become due.

HOW DUE-NESS WORKS. A family is enqueued when its due score, credit_mean multiplied by staleness and divided by budget, clears the threshold of one, and when it is affordable, meaning its budget is at or below one minus the load bucket divided by three. Staleness is therefore the only term that can move a resting family toward firing. Credit changes slowly with outcomes and budget is fixed.

THE DEFECT. The resolver named in edit_site recomputes staleness for the gap-closing family only. That is stated plainly in its own comment. Every other family keeps whatever staleness it was seeded with, permanently. Measured immediately after restoration: eleven considered, zero enqueued, zero skipped, with the affordable families sitting at staleness between 0.05 and 0.13 and therefore scoring far below the threshold.

THE TRAP THIS CREATES. The one family that does have a driver is gap-closing, whose staleness correctly reads one because there are over a thousand open gaps. But its budget is 0.40 and the affordability ceiling at a load bucket of two is 0.333, so the only family that can become due is also the one that is priced out of firing under ordinary load. The result is a scheduler that is internally coherent and completely inert.

PROPOSED CHANGE, minimal and mechanical. For any family with no reality-derived staleness read, grow staleness as a function of time since that family last fired, saturating at one, and reset it on fire. This is the same fire-then-decay economics the existing family already follows, merely supplied by elapsed time rather than by a measured backlog, and it requires no new judgement about what any family is worth. Families that do gain a real reality read later can override it.

WHAT MUST NOT BE CONCLUDED FROM A RESTORED REGISTRY. The observable that matters is enqueued greater than zero, not rhythms greater than zero. Reporting the restoration as a recovered cadence would have been wrong, and was nearly reported that way.

OUT OF SCOPE HERE, and an operator decision rather than a defect: whether gap-closing's budget of 0.40 against a ceiling of 0.333 is the approved economics working as designed, deliberately making expensive work wait for capacity, or a mis-tuning that starves the highest-value family. That is a threshold judgement and is deliberately not decided in this gap.

FALSIFIER. Count enqueued entries returned by the conductor across a day. It is currently zero across every observed tick with eleven families considered. This gap is closed when a family other than gap-closing is enqueued at least once without an operator changing any budget by hand.

summary:
The enumerated-anchor mechanism that makes a fabricated anchor impossible exists in this file and is wired only to the path the failures do not take. Extending it to the primary drafting path is the single highest-leverage change available to the authoring lane.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS. In the re-derivation block, feature-compose.ts offers the model a numbered list of verified-unique anchors and takes the bytes from OUR list rather than from the model's output. Its own comment states the principle: "let it pick an INDEX and take the bytes from the verified list here. The anchor then CANNOT be invented, because the model never writes it." That block also handles the details correctly — an indexed answer wins over free text, the window-provenance check is deliberately skipped for an indexed anchor because such an anchor has better provenance than the window test, a single-candidate list is auto-accepted, and every check fails open.

WHERE IT IS NOT. The identifier `anchor_index` occurs at exactly four lines in this file, ALL inside that re-derivation block. The PRIMARY drafting path still asks the model to reproduce an anchor as text: it logs "[fc-anchors] supplied verified-unique anchors for <path> (N locator candidate(s))" and then requests a verbatim old_string. The drafter demonstrably paraphrases what it is shown — measured on src/seed/index.ts, an untouched file: the source has `export const SEED_TEMPLATES: ActivityTemplate[] = [` and the model returned it without the type annotation; the source has `export { X } from "./add-resolver-to-vessel.js";` and the model returned it without the from-clause. Indentation is altered the same way.

PROMPT-LEVEL CORRECTION HAS BEEN TRIED AND DOES NOT WORK ON THIS CLASS. Commit 12c4c58 added an explicit instruction not to return the failed anchor, and the very next repair echoed it anyway. The re-derivation comment reaches the same conclusion independently: "A model that ignores a list will ignore a longer one, so stop asking it to reproduce a string at all." The lever must be mechanical.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING. Hard anchor failure (apply_failed with ops_applied == 0) accounts for roughly 28% of compose attempts, and the composer's own rate has sat at 20-23% since 2026-09-08 against a 10-12% baseline on 09-05/06. This is the dominant loss in the authoring lane.

SHAPE OF THE CHANGE. Two sites must move together, which is why it has not happened incrementally: the drafting prompt must render the verified-unique anchors as an INDEXED list with an instruction to answer with an index, and the plan-application path must resolve an op's anchor_index against that same list before falling back to op.old_string. Both halves must be in one change; a prompt that offers indices to an applier that ignores them is worse than neither, because the model will spend its answer on a field that is dropped.

DO NOT THREAD THE LIST THROUGH FUNCTION SIGNATURES. Two prior attempts on this file died on cross-scope bindings (TS2339, TS2304) and one on changing a return type without changing its declaration (TS2322: returning {text, conceptIds} from a function still declared Promise<string>). Use a module-scoped array holding the last rendered anchor list for the file being planned, written where the list is built and read where the op is applied. Anchor every edit on a single short line; measured landing on this file collapses as anchor length grows.

FAIL OPEN, AND CHANGE NOTHING ELSE. An absent, non-numeric or out-of-range index must fall through to today's exact behaviour, so the change can only add a path and never remove one. Preserve the existing uniqueness check and refuseRederivedEdit call unchanged.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. The claim is not that the code contains a new identifier. It is that the hard anchor-failure rate falls. compose-drift-tick already measures exactly this population (apply_failed AND ops_applied == 0 over feature_compose executions, day-scale) against the composer's own median baseline, so the closure test is a sustained fall in that rate on complete days after the change lands, with the day the change landed recorded. Note this file has NO TEST FILE, so every gate reads the diff and none executes it; a FAVORABLE verdict here means reviewed, not run.

In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/rhythm-reality-sync.ts, stop writing a fabricated zero when the open-gap count could not be read. One file, one concern.

Two anchors, each occurring exactly once.

Anchor A, indented with two spaces:
  let openGapCount = 0;
Immediately after it, declare a sibling boolean initialised false, named openGapKnown.

Anchor B, indented with six spaces:
      openGapCount = typeof data?.body?.open === "number" ? data.body.open : 0;
Rewrite that single statement so that the numeric field is assigned to openGapCount and openGapKnown is set true ONLY when the field is actually a number. When it is not, leave openGapCount at its initial value and leave openGapKnown false. Do not set openGapKnown anywhere else: the surrounding catch block and the non-ok response path must both leave it false.

Then find the point where the new staleness is computed from openGapCount and written back, and make the whole recompute-and-write step conditional on openGapKnown being true. When it is false, skip the computation and the write entirely so the stored staleness keeps its previous value.

Finally, include openGapKnown in the returned report body under the name open_gap_known, so a caller can distinguish an abstention from a genuine empty backlog.

Why this is required, precisely. Zero is not a neutral placeholder here. The value feeds staleness as the minimum of one and the count divided by a target backlog, so a zero writes a staleness of zero, which states that the family whose job is draining gaps has nothing to do. When the read fails the truth is that the count is unknown, and unknown is not empty. There are currently over a thousand open gaps, and a single failed read was enough to mark that family idle. Preserving the last known-good value on failure is correct; fabricating a zero destroys it.

Do not change the computation used when the count IS known, do not alter the request timeout, do not touch other rhythm families, and edit no other file.

THE ATTRIBUTION IS FALSE, AND THE CONTROL IS CHEAP. The edited file is src/resolvers/learning-signal-health-observer.ts; the failing test exercises test/resolvers/vessel-mitosis-cutover.test.ts. There is no import path between them, and the deleted constants were read by nothing. Running that test file on a CLEAN tree with no draft applied reproduces the failure:

    (fail) vessel_mitosis_cutover > freshness gate: refuses cutover when staged_base_sha is missing [5001.02ms]
    (fail) vessel_mitosis_cutover > git-aware cutover: applies staged files, commits, mirrors to /vessels [5001.60ms]
    21 pass, 2 fail

THE MECHANISM IS A TIMEOUT, NOT AN ASSERTION. Both durations are 5001ms against a 5000ms limit. These tests spawn git and filesystem work and are load-sensitive: in a quiet baseline run they pass, and during a compose - which is running typechecks and model calls concurrently, at a host load average around 8 - they exceed the limit. That is why the reproduction check confirms rather than filters them: the second run happens under the same load as the first, so a slow test is slow twice. "Reproduced" is being read as "caused by the draft" when it only establishes "not a one-off flake".

WHY THIS MATTERS. The gate is the last thing standing between a correct change and a landing, and it is rejecting on a signal unrelated to the change. The composer's own hard anchor-failure rate has been measured at 20-23% since 2026-09-08 against a 10-12% baseline; if a share of the remaining verdict losses are false blocks of this kind, effort spent on the drafter and the judge is aimed at the wrong component. It also interacts badly with the fact that this vessel currently carries 28 pre-existing test failures out of 2,235: a noisy baseline makes every comparison less reliable.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. Distinguish a timeout from an assertion failure before attributing it: a test that fails by exceeding its time limit is not evidence about a diff unless the diff plausibly touches its execution path. At minimum, exclude timeout-class failures from newly-failing attribution and report them separately as an environment signal; better, re-run a suspected new failure in isolation, unloaded, before blocking on it, since an isolated re-run is exactly what distinguishes the two. Raising the limit on these specific tests would also work but treats one instance rather than the class.

NOTE THE COMPLEMENTARY DEFECT ALREADY KNOWN. computeNewlyFailing returns NO new failures when the baseline is null or empty, so it fails open in one direction and, as shown here, false-blocks in the other. Both stem from treating a noisy comparison as authoritative.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. Dispatch a provably inert change - for example deleting an unused local - and confirm it is not blocked by a failing test in a file with no import relationship to the edited module. Reading the source cannot establish this; it needs the compose report.

SECOND INSTANCE, 2026-09-10 ~11:40, AND THIS ONE BLOCKED A DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY CHANGE.

Compose route-edit-e40558ea, one op against repos/ias-executor-ts/src/adapters/activity-api-provider.ts. The change adds a single console.warn to a branch that already returns null, so it cannot alter control flow or any value. The compose report records:

    apply_failed: false          <- the edit applied cleanly
    op_count: 1                  <- single operation
    rolled_back: true
    semantic_gate.addresses: null <- the judge NEVER RAN
    summary: "deterministic edit synthesized from the goal's verbatim old→new replacement"

Note the summary: the composer recognised a verbatim old→new pair and synthesized the edit DETERMINISTICALLY, with no model drafting involved. So this is the cleanest possible case — a one-line, machine-synthesized, provably inert diagnostic — and it was still refused, before any semantic judgement, by the gate that precedes it.

WHY THIS INSTANCE MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIRST. The change being blocked is the one that makes this class of failure diagnosable at all: it adds the missing log line to ActivityApiTemplateProvider.getTemplate, whose silent nulls are why a template that activity-api serves with HTTP 200 is reported by goal-host as absent, and why that investigation took seven hypotheses. So the test gate is currently blocking the instrumentation needed to diagnose a separate defect - a false block with a compounding cost, not merely a wasted draft.

TWO ATTEMPTS, SAME OUTCOME. Dispatched twice, roughly forty minutes apart, both reaching fc-plan and neither producing a semantic verdict. That rules out a one-off: whatever the gate is comparing against is failing this diff consistently, and consistently for reasons unrelated to the diff, which is exactly the failure mode this gap describes.

THE SECOND INSTANCE IS NOT A TIMEOUT — IT IS A CORRUPTED TEST TREE, AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT AND WORSE MECHANISM.

Reading the verify block of route-edit-e40558ea rather than assuming it matched the first instance:

    compose environment:   134 pass, 32 fail, 30 ERRORS, 166 tests across 46 files
    clean tree, same repo:  372 pass, 23 fail,  0 errors, 395 tests across 50 files

The compose ran FEWER FILES (46 vs 50) and produced 30 ERRORS. Errors at that count are module-load failures, not assertion failures and not timeouts. A one-line console.warn added to a branch that already returns null cannot remove four test files from a run or prevent modules from loading.

The gate's own message names the symptom precisely — "PASSING TESTS DISAPPEARED: 353 -> 134 (a draft must not delete coverage or break module load to go green)" — and that rule is CORRECT. A draft really must not delete coverage. The defect is the attribution: the coverage vanished for a reason the draft did not cause, and the gate has no way to tell the difference.

THE LIKELY CAUSE TIES THIS TO THE CONCURRENT-COMPOSE CLASS. Composes share working trees; this substrate has already recorded both directions of that contention — "SKIPPING ROLLBACK ... file content has changed (likely by another concurrent compose)" on the refusal side, and a cutover committing another gap's staged edit under its own attribution on the landing side. A third consequence follows directly: another compose's IN-FLIGHT, HALF-APPLIED edit sitting in the shared tree while this draft's suite runs will break module load for whatever files import it, and every one of those failures is then attributed to the draft under test.

That converts an intermittent nuisance into a systematic one. It is not load-sensitive and not random: it fires whenever two composes overlap on one vessel, which on a continuously-running lane is most of the time. It also explains why two attempts forty minutes apart failed identically — not a flake reproducing, but a shared tree that was dirty on both occasions.

NOTE ALSO: the clean tree carries 23 pre-existing failures of its own. So the baseline this gate differences against is noisy even before contention, which is the condition the original entry above describes.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY, REVISED. Run the same provably-inert one-line diff twice: once while no other compose touches that vessel, and once during a concurrent compose on it. If the first passes and the second reports vanished coverage, the attribution defect is contention, not flake, and the fix is isolation of the test tree rather than better flake filtering.

summary:
The recovery ladder's third rung asks a present-tense question, are landed changes known to do something, but computes it as an all-time sum with no time filter. The consequence is that a genuine improvement in coverage cannot move it for more than a day, so the rung cannot observe its own repair.

THE MEASUREMENT. The rung sums the examined and uncovered target counts over every execution carrying that metadata, with no executed_at bound. Its sibling rungs in the same resolver DO bound their queries by time, using a one hour and a one day window, so this rung is the outlier rather than the convention.

MEASURED EFFECT OF A REAL FIX. After a coverage fix deployed at 08:08 on 2026-09-10, composes running since that moment report ten targets examined and two uncovered, a covered fraction of 0.80. The all-time figure the rung actually reads is 1174 examined and 757 uncovered, a covered fraction of 0.355, and the rung holds only at 0.5 or above. Crossing that threshold at the observed post-fix rate requires roughly 567 further examinations, which at current compose throughput is well over a day of continuous work. The improvement is real, measurable, and invisible to the instrument that exists to detect it.

WHY THIS IS FILED RATHER THAN CHANGED. I considered windowing this rung earlier in the same session and rejected it, because at that time the windowed values were WORSE than the all-time average: one day read 0.281 and one hour read 0.091 against an all-time 0.351. The same change now would flip the rung in favour of work I just did. A measurement change that is proposed only once it flatters the proposer is not a measurement change worth trusting, regardless of how sound the underlying argument is. The argument should be judged on its merits by someone other than the party it benefits, which is why this is a gap and not a dispatch.

THE ARGUMENT ON ITS MERITS, stated plainly so it can be judged. A present-tense question deserves a bounded window. An all-time average of a quantity that only ever accumulates means any period of poor behaviour is permanent, and the rung's ability to report improvement decays as the corpus grows. The counter-argument is equally real: a short window is noisy, and a rung that flips on ten samples is not a stable signal. A defensible middle is a window long enough to be stable and short enough to move, reported alongside the all-time figure rather than replacing it, so a reader can see both the current rate and the accumulated history.

FALSIFIER. Compare the covered fraction computed over a bounded recent window against the all-time figure the rung publishes. The gap is closed when the rung reports a value that responds to a change in current behaviour within a working day, whether by windowing, by reporting both figures, or by an alternative that preserves the same property.

summary:
CORRECTED 2026-09-10 after investigation. The earlier headline of this gap — "its template is absent from the catalogue" — is WRONG and withdrawn. The template is present, active and fetchable. The real finding is narrower and splits in two.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE.

  The template is in the catalogue and has been since 2026-09-09T09:41:32Z. It is
  retrievable with HTTP 200 at the endpoint the executor's adapter actually uses,
  GET /v2/activities/templates/development-vessel%3Agate-self-probe-tick. It carries
  proposed=false, deprecated=false, retired=false, execution_type=template. Three
  earlier 404s were wrong URLs (/activities/:id, /templates/:id), not absence — a
  false zero from guessing an endpoint instead of reading the adapter.

  Its tags are the sanitized form the catalogue requires (intenthorizondetection,
  boredomtargettemplate, ...) because the catalogue TagSchema rejects colons and
  underscores. That is NOT a defect: the boredom selector explicitly matches BOTH
  forms — `tags.includes("boredom_target_template") || tags.includes("boredomtargettemplate")` —
  and queries FTS on the collapsed form. Eligibility is intact.

DEFECT 1 — IT IS ELIGIBLE AND NEVER SELECTED. The probe has executed exactly ONCE in
its life: 2026-09-09T09:41:42Z, ten seconds after its own creation, i.e. the operator
dispatch that created it. Nothing since, across 25 hours and thousands of fleet
executions. It is correctly catalogued, correctly tagged, not deprecated, not retired,
and boredom-eligible — and selection simply never picks it. This is not a wiring bug.
It is the selection-dormancy class already measured on 2026-09-09, when 90 of 102
validator-shaped activities were dormant and every survivor was timer-driven while
every dormant one was selection-scheduled. The gate self-probe is one more instance:
the substrate's only known-answer detector of gate regressions rides a selector that
has no obligation to run it.

DEFECT 2 — IT CANNOT BE FORCED EITHER. Dispatching it by pin fails:
POST /run-goal {"targetTemplateId":"development-vessel:gate-self-probe-tick"} returns
"GoalHost.runGoal: template '...' not found in shared catalogue or activity-api",
while that same id returns HTTP 200 from activity-api's template endpoint moments
later. goal-host resolves templates through a live call (getTemplateLocalFirst → local
provider, else the hub adapter), not a boot cache, so a stale cache does not explain
it. Something in that lookup chain fails for a template the catalogue serves. This is
the defect that matters operationally: with selection not choosing the probe and the
pin path refusing it, there is NO way to run it — neither autonomously nor on demand.

WHY THIS MATTERS. gate_self_probe is the known-answer corpus: hostile fixtures that
must be refused with citations, benign controls that must pass, run through the REAL
exported gate functions. It is the cheapest possible detector of gate regressions, and
it is the probe a learning-loop selftest must dispatch to verify the execution→learning
chain end to end. Both of its routes are closed, so the substrate currently has no way
to check its own gates, and the selftest runner cannot be committed against it.

FOUR HYPOTHESES DIED ON THE WAY HERE, RECORDED SO THEY ARE NOT RETRIED: (a) the
template is absent from the catalogue — false, it is fetchable; (b) the upload fails on
tag format — true of the WRITE contract but not the cause of dormancy, and an earlier
"refutation" of this was itself invalid because it used the wrong request envelope;
(c) activityTemplate_write only proposes — false, proposed=false on the live row;
(d) the sanitized tag breaks boredom matching — false, the selector accepts both forms.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. Two independent assertions, both required: a pin dispatch by
targetTemplateId must succeed rather than returning not-found, AND the execution count
for gate-self-probe must rise above 1 without an operator trigger. Reading the seed
file or the catalogue row proves neither — both have been correct the whole time.

DEFECT 2 IS NOW ISOLATED TO goal-host, WITH FOUR CONFOUNDS RULED OUT. Measured 2026-09-10 10:44, twenty minutes after the catalogue row was independently confirmed:

  Endpoint config   goal-host's process env has ACTIVITY_API_ENDPOINT,
                    ACTIVITY_API_URL, PRODUCER_DISCOVERY_ENDPOINT and
                    METABOB_ENDPOINT ALL set to http://127.0.0.1:8080. There is no
                    misdirected local-vs-hub endpoint; both paths point at
                    activity-api.

  Reachability      From INSIDE the container, with goal-host's own API key:
                    GET http://127.0.0.1:8080/v2/activities/templates/development-vessel%3Agate-self-probe-tick
                    returns HTTP 200 and the template body. The unencoded-colon form
                    also returns 200. So the row is reachable by the exact call the
                    adapter makes, from the exact process environment.

  Caching           goal-host resolves live: getTemplateLocalFirst tries the local
                    provider then falls through to the hub adapter, both HTTP. There
                    is no boot-time template cache to be stale.

  Timing            The first failure was 16s after the write and could plausibly have
                    raced it. This one is 20 minutes later, against a row confirmed
                    present in the same minute. Not a race.

  And it still returns: "GoalHost.runGoal: template
  'development-vessel:gate-self-probe-tick' not found in shared catalogue or
  activity-api".

So a template that activity-api serves with 200, to goal-host's own credentials, from
goal-host's own network namespace, is reported by goal-host as absent from
activity-api. The fault is in the lookup chain inside goal-host or the executor
library's CatalogueWithFallback, not in the catalogue, the credentials, the endpoint
configuration, or the request timing. Locating the precise line requires reading that
chain in ias-executor-ts and is the next step.

OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE, RESTATED PRECISELY. Selection never picks this probe (defect
1) and the pin path refuses it (defect 2), so the only detector the substrate has for
gate regressions cannot be run by any route — not autonomously, and not by an operator
who knows its exact id. Any future selftest of the execution→learning chain is blocked
on defect 2 specifically, because a selftest must be able to dispatch its own probe on
demand rather than wait to be selected.

DEFECT 2 NARROWED TO ONE BRANCH. Reading the lookup chain end to end eliminated three more candidate explanations, each of which looked right until it was checked:

  The local-first wrapper is INACTIVE here, by design and correctly. goal-host wraps
  host.activityApi.getTemplate only when PRODUCER_DISCOVERY_ENDPOINT differs from
  ACTIVITY_API_ENDPOINT; measured, both are http://127.0.0.1:8080, so localTemplateApi
  is null and the wrap is a documented no-op passthrough. Not the cause.

  The negative cache CANNOT hold a stale null this long. CatalogueWithFallback keeps a
  remoteCache whose negative TTL is Math.min(5_000, ttl) — five seconds. Dispatches were
  minutes and hours apart. Not the cause.

  The remote fetch DID NOT FAIL. ActivityApiAdapter documents "getTemplate on non-2xx →
  returns null and logs warning". goal-host's journal carries NO such warning around any
  of the failed dispatches. So the adapter did not receive a non-2xx.

WHAT IS LEFT, STATED AS THE ONLY REMAINING BRANCH. CatalogueWithFallback.getTemplate
asks the in-memory local provider first and returns on a hit; on a miss it consults the
remote and returns `remote ? normalize(remote) : null`. Given the row is served 200 to
goal-host's own credentials from its own namespace, and no non-2xx warning was logged,
the failure is either that the remote call is not reached on this path, or that a 200
response is normalized to null. Distinguishing those requires instrumenting that
function or reading the normalizer against this template's exact body — the shape has
`id: "activity:⟨development-vessel:gate-self-probe-tick⟩"` with the wrapper braces,
which is a plausible normalization trip-hazard worth checking first.

SEVEN HYPOTHESES, SIX REFUTED. Recorded so the next attempt starts from the branch above
rather than re-walking: template absent from catalogue (fetchable 200); tag format causes
dormancy (write contract only, and the first "refutation" was itself invalid — wrong
envelope); activityTemplate_write only proposes (proposed=false on the live row);
sanitized tags break boredom matching (selector accepts both forms); endpoint
misconfiguration (all four env vars agree); stale negative cache (5s TTL). What survives
is a single unexamined branch, which is a better starting point than any of the six.

CORRECTION, AND THE ACTUAL ROOT DEFECT. An earlier entry above concluded "the remote fetch DID NOT FAIL" because no adapter warning appears in goal-host's journal. THAT INFERENCE IS WITHDRAWN. It rested on ActivityApiAdapter's own docstring, which states "getTemplate on non-2xx → returns null and logs warning". The provider it delegates to does not log:

    async getTemplate(templateId: string): Promise<ActivityTemplate | null> {
      const url = `${this.endpoint}/v2/activities/templates/${encodeURIComponent(templateId)}`;
      const res = await globalThis.fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: `ApiKey ${this.apiKey}` } });
      if (!res.ok) {
        try { await res.body?.cancel(); } catch { /* swallow */ }
        return null;                       // silent
      }
      const raw = await res.json() as RawTemplate;
      try { await res.body?.cancel(); } catch { /* swallow */ }
      if (!raw?.id) return null;           // also silent

Both failure paths return null with no log line, and the transport error path is not caught here at all. So the absence of a warning is not evidence about the fetch, and this whole investigation's difficulty follows from that: a template that is genuinely missing, a fetch that 404s, a fetch that 500s, and a 200 whose body lacks `id` are ALL indistinguishable from outside — they produce the same null and the same downstream message, "not found in shared catalogue or activity-api", which names two sources without saying which one was consulted or what either answered.

THIS IS THE DEFECT TO FIX FIRST, AHEAD OF THE TEMPLATE ITSELF. Not because the silent null is the root cause of the dormancy — it may or may not be — but because while it stands, no one can tell which cause is operating. Three lines of logging at those two returns (status code and url on non-2xx, and a distinct line for a 200 whose body has no id) converts an undiagnosable failure into a one-line answer, and would have ended this investigation at its first step instead of its seventh.

It is also the same class this substrate keeps producing, one level deeper than usual: a DOCUMENTED behaviour that does not exist. The docstring asserts a warning; the code returns silently; every reader downstream — including this investigation — trusted the docstring over the implementation. "Verify at the layer that consumes the artifact" applies to documentation too.

THE FIX CANNOT BE DELIVERED BY THE ORDINARY LANE, AND THAT IS THE LARGER FINDING. The silent-null returns live in ias-executor-ts, a LIBRARY consumed via a file: dependency. goal-host's copy declares "main": "./dist/index.js", and dist carries its own compiled copy of that provider. So a compose that edits repos/ias-executor-ts/src lands correct source that the runtime never loads: the change would be committed, pushed, gated green, and INERT.

That is not a hypothesis about this gap; it is the same defect already recorded on this substrate as six inert guards that all passed their checks against the wrong artifact. What it means here is narrower and sharper: the ordinary edit-intent → compose → mitosis-cutover path CANNOT change executor behaviour. It can only change vessel source. Delivering a library fix additionally requires a build of dist and a redeploy of the consuming vessels, which no lane in this system performs as part of landing a change.

CONSEQUENCE FOR SELF-MODIFICATION, STATED PLAINLY. The substrate can rewrite its vessels but not the engine they run on. Every defect that lives in ias-executor-ts — the silent null here, and anything else in the execution core — is outside what autonomous self-development can reach, no matter how well the gap is written or how correct the drafted patch is. A gap filed against a library file will attract composes that land and change nothing, consuming authoring capacity and producing green verdicts for inert work. Anyone filing against repos/ias-executor-ts should know that before dispatching, and the compose lane arguably ought to refuse such targets outright rather than land into them.

SO THE ORDER FOR THIS GAP IS: (1) add the two log lines in the library source and REBUILD dist, by hand or through whatever build lane exists, since no compose will do it; (2) with the failure finally legible, read which of the four indistinguishable causes is actually operating; (3) fix that; (4) only then re-attempt the selftest runner, whose Phase-1 probe this unblocks.

WITHDRAWN: "THE SUBSTRATE CANNOT MODIFY THE ENGINE IT RUNS ON". The entry immediately above claimed the fix is undeliverable because no lane rebuilds dist, and concluded that library defects are structurally outside autonomous self-development. That claim was asserted without checking and is FALSE.

substrate-pull-sync does exactly this job, and was hardened for precisely this failure. When a shared package with a build script changes, it finds the consumers that file:-dep it, builds to a staging dir, refuses to touch a single consumer if the build fails (keeping the live dist and emitting its own gap), swaps dist only on success, and then PROPAGATES BY CONTENT rather than assuming symlinks. Its own comment records why that last part exists — measured 2026-08-16 on @avigopal/ias-executor-ts:

    development-vessel   realfiles=0    symlinks=164   <- propagated
    ribosome-vessel      realfiles=164  symlinks=0     <- frozen at 08-05
    goal-host-vessel / analysis-vessel / llm-resolver-vessel / local-tools-vessel
                         realfiles=164  symlinks=0     <- frozen at 08-05

Five of six consumers were frozen for eleven days, health checks passed throughout because a consumer running stale code is perfectly healthy, and the run logged "fan-out healthy" while disarming the very retry meant to catch it. That defect was found and fixed. So the delivery path for a library change is: edit src, push, pull-sync rebuilds dist, content-propagates to every consumer, bounces them.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE ORDERING ABOVE. The logging fix IS deliverable through the ordinary path, and the step-1 caveat ("by hand, since no compose will do it") is withdrawn with it. The genuine caveat is smaller and worth keeping: the rebuild happens in pull-sync, not in the compose/cutover that lands the edit, so a library change is green-and-inert in the window BETWEEN landing and the next pull-sync tick — and the dist-freshness check is what closes that window, not the compose gate.

EIGHTH HYPOTHESIS, ALSO MINE, ALSO REFUTED BY READING RATHER THAN ASSERTING. The pattern across this gap is now consistent enough to name: every time a mechanism appeared missing, it existed and was either unreachable, unlogged, or unverified — never absent. The substrate's problem in this investigation has not once been a missing mechanism.

[narrowed from two-named-capabilities-in-the-goal-host-are-exported-imported-and-never-invoked] Two fully implemented, exported capabilities in goal-host-vessel are imported by src/index.ts and invoked nowhere. The type checker can see both and was never asked.

WHAT IS DEAD, AND HOW IT WAS FOUND. Running the vessel's own tsc with --noUnusedLocals --noUnusedParameters (flags that are NOT enabled fleet-wide) reports 12 unused symbols against a baseline of 0 errors. Two of them are not incidental:

  inferGoalTargetShapes - defined and exported at src/goal-target-inference.ts:87,
  imported at src/index.ts:260, and referenced elsewhere only inside comments
  (goal-target-inference.ts:211, :891 and index.ts:3728). Never invoked. Its
  sibling on the SAME import line, inferGoalTargetDecision, IS used, so the module
  is live and there are two target-inference entry points of which only one is wired.

  decideContinuation - the sole export of src/walk-continuation.ts, declared at :45,
  imported at src/index.ts:276, referenced nowhere else. Never invoked. An entire
  walk-continuation module with no caller.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN TWO UNUSED IMPORTS. These are not helpers. "Infer the target shapes of a goal" and "decide whether the walk continues" name two of the goal host's core reasoning steps. Anyone reading this vessel to understand how a goal acquires its targets would land on inferGoalTargetShapes and conclude they had found the path. They would be reading code that does not execute. The same is true of walk-continuation for anyone asking how the walk decides to stop.

THIS IS THE SAME CLASS THE SUBSTRATE KEEPS PRODUCING. A mechanism is built correctly, and nothing connects it to a caller: the rhythm registry built and empty; the regionHint consumer complete at low producer coverage; compose-lesson credit wired to the wrong drafter; a learning-signal detector permanently gated by a volume floor its own source cannot clear; enumerated anchor choice implemented only on the path the failures do not take. This is that pattern again, and unlike the others it is visible to a compiler flag rather than requiring a live probe.

NOT A REQUEST TO DELETE THEM. Which way to resolve each is a judgement this gap does not make. inferGoalTargetShapes may be the better of the two inference paths and the wiring may be what is missing; or it may be superseded by inferGoalTargetDecision and should go. Same for decideContinuation. What is not defensible is leaving a named, exported, imported capability that never runs, because it reads as wired to every future reader and to every drafter that greps this file.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. For each symbol, either a call site exists on an executing path, or the symbol and its now-unused import are gone. Reading the definition proves nothing - the definitions are already there and already correct.

RELATED, AND THE REASON THIS WAS INVISIBLE. noUnusedLocals is not enabled in any vessel. Surveyed 2026-09-10: goal-host 12 violations, ias-executor-ts 19, development-vessel 75, activity-api 159, every baseline 0. Enabling the flags would surface this class permanently, but must follow clearing the existing violations, since enabling first fails typecheck and blocks every compose against that vessel.

[narrowed from ten-of-eleven-rhythm-families-have-no-staleness-driver] The rhythm registry was restored on 2026-09-10 and the conductor reads all eleven families, yet nothing is ever enqueued. The cause is not the registry and not the conductor: ten of the eleven families have no mechanism by which their staleness can ever rise, so they can never become due.

HOW DUE-NESS WORKS. A family is enqueued when its due score, credit_mean multiplied by staleness and divided by budget, clears the threshold of one, and when it is affordable, meaning its budget is at or below one minus the load bucket divided by three. Staleness is therefore the only term that can move a resting family toward firing. Credit changes slowly with outcomes and budget is fixed.

THE DEFECT. The resolver named in edit_site recomputes staleness for the gap-closing family only. That is stated plainly in its own comment. Every other family keeps whatever staleness it was seeded with, permanently. Measured immediately after restoration: eleven considered, zero enqueued, zero skipped, with the affordable families sitting at staleness between 0.05 and 0.13 and therefore scoring far below the threshold.

THE TRAP THIS CREATES. The one family that does have a driver is gap-closing, whose staleness correctly reads one because there are over a thousand open gaps. But its budget is 0.40 and the affordability ceiling at a load bucket of two is 0.333, so the only family that can become due is also the one that is priced out of firing under ordinary load. The result is a scheduler that is internally coherent and completely inert.

PROPOSED CHANGE, minimal and mechanical. For any family with no reality-derived staleness read, grow staleness as a function of time since that family last fired, saturating at one, and reset it on fire. This is the same fire-then-decay economics the existing family already follows, merely supplied by elapsed time rather than by a measured backlog, and it requires no new judgement about what any family is worth. Families that do gain a real reality read later can override it.

WHAT MUST NOT BE CONCLUDED FROM A RESTORED REGISTRY. The observable that matters is enqueued greater than zero, not rhythms greater than zero. Reporting the restoration as a recovered cadence would have been wrong, and was nearly reported that way.

OUT OF SCOPE HERE, and an operator decision rather than a defect: whether gap-closing's budget of 0.40 against a ceiling of 0.333 is the approved economics working as designed, deliberately making expensive work wait for capacity, or a mis-tuning that starves the highest-value family. That is a threshold judgement and is deliberately not decided in this gap.

FALSIFIER. Count enqueued entries returned by the conductor across a day. It is currently zero across every observed tick with eleven families considered. This gap is closed when a family other than gap-closing is enqueued at least once without an operator changing any budget by hand.

summary:
The effect-coverage check that drives the recovery ladder's third rung resolves every path under the workspace root, and for a submodule vessel that path is a working tree nothing keeps current. It is currently up to 25 days stale, so tests added to those vessels are structurally invisible to the check and the rung cannot rise however many are written.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. The check builds candidate and fallback paths from the workspace root, which in the running vessel resolves to the super-repo checkout. Three trees exist per vessel in that container and only one is fresh. The super-repo submodule tree for the goal host sits at a commit dated 2026-08-16. The clone that the pull-sync loop actually fast-forwards sits at 2026-09-10 and does contain the test added that day. The runtime tree carries source only. The check reads the first of those three.

A POINTER BUMP DOES NOT REPAIR IT. The super-repo pointers were advanced and pull-sync pulled the commit: the container super-repo moved forward and the recorded pointer for the goal host correctly reads the new revision. The checked-out files did not move, and the super-repo reports the submodule entry as modified. Pull-sync advances the super-repo but never updates submodule working trees, so the recorded pointer and the files on disk disagree indefinitely.

SCOPE. Seven of fourteen vessels are drifted, by four to twenty-five days, and the undrifted ones are the inactive vessels. The actively developed vessels are exactly the drifted ones, which is the worst possible correlation for a checker that measures development.

THIS IS NOT A NEW DRIFT. A test committed on 2026-08-05 in the goal host records the same measurement, nine of eighteen vessels drifted at that time, and it was written because a file-count goal answered against the stale tree and the walk credited the answer as deterministically verified. The drift is a month old and known. What is new is that the coverage check feeding the ladder now reads the same stale tree, so a second consumer has been captured by the same fossil.

EVIDENCE THAT THE READER IS THE PROBLEM RATHER THAN THE TESTS. Five coverage changes were made on 2026-09-10. Exactly one became visible to the check within minutes, and it is the one in the vessel that is a plain directory inside the super-repo rather than a submodule. The other four are present in the fresh clones and absent from the trees the check reads.

PROPOSED CHANGE, smaller option first. Point the coverage check at the fresh clone when resolving a submodule vessel path, leaving every other reader untouched. The broader alternative is to have the sync loop update submodule working trees after advancing the super-repo, which fixes every super-repo-relative reader at once but changes what all of them see and therefore carries more risk.

FALSIFIER. For a vessel whose submodule tree is behind its clone, add a test file to that vessel and confirm the coverage check counts the corresponding target as covered within one sync cycle. It currently does not, and the gap is closed when it does.

summary:
A compose cutover for one gap committed another gap's staged edit under its own attribution, and mirrored only its own files — leaving the swept-in change present in git and absent from the running tree.

OBSERVED 2026-09-10 11:11:17. An operator dispatch edited repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/patch-with-tools.ts, adding a diagnostic to the semantic gate's PASSED log line. It reached origin/dev inside commit 2a5a305, whose message is "substrate-authored: apply recommit-ten-of-eleven-rhythm-families-have-no-staleness-driver-syntax_break-compose-report via mitosis cutover" — a completely unrelated gap about rhythm staleness drivers. `git log -S` confirms 2a5a305 is the commit that introduced the line; the operator's own dispatch produced no commit of its own.

TWO DISTINCT DEFECTS, BOTH FOLLOWING FROM THE SAME CAUSE.

  1. MIS-ATTRIBUTED LANDING. The commit says it applies the rhythm-families gap and
     in fact carries an unrelated change to the patcher's logging. Anyone asking
     "what did this gap change?" — an operator, a closure predicate, the gap store's
     own durability accounting, a future bisect — gets a wrong answer. Worse, the
     compose that owns the commit never judged the change it carried: the semantic
     gate that ran, ran against the rhythm-families patch.

  2. GIT AHEAD OF RUNTIME. The cutover mirrored its own staged files to /vessels and
     not the swept-in one. Measured immediately after: origin/dev contains the line,
     /vessels/development-vessel/src/resolvers/patch-with-tools.ts does not, and the
     vessel restarted at 11:11:36 — after the 11:11:17 commit — so the restart did
     not carry it either. The runtime is behind git for that file until the next
     pull-sync reconciles it.

THIS IS THE CONCURRENT-COMPOSE CLASS IN THE LANDING DIRECTION. The same root cause is
already recorded on the refusal side: "SKIPPING ROLLBACK ... file content has changed
(likely by another concurrent compose)", where a refused compose's bytes survive
because another compose touched the file. Here the same shared-tree contention runs
forward instead of backward: whichever compose reaches cutover first commits whatever
is in the tree, including work it did not author and did not gate.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. Every accounting this substrate keeps about its own
self-modification is attribution-based — which gap closed, which compose landed, which
lane authored what. Commit attribution is the substrate's ONLY durable record of that,
and it is wrong whenever two composes overlap on one vessel. It also silently defeats
the one-operation-per-plan discipline that the partial-landing evidence recommends: a
plan can be atomic and still arrive inside someone else's commit.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. Dispatch two edits to different files in the same vessel so their
composes overlap, then check that each resulting commit contains only the ops of the
gap it names, and that /vessels matches origin/dev for every file the commit touched.
Reading the cutover source is not sufficient — the contention is a timing property.

CORRECTION — DEFECT 2 IS TRANSIENT, NOT A PERMANENT SPLIT. The entry above described the swept-in change as present in git and absent from the running tree, which was true at the moment of measurement and overstated as a standing condition. Watched to resolution: substrate-pull-sync reconciled it on its next tick.

    11:11:17  commit 2a5a305 lands, carrying the swept-in edit
    11:11:36  vessel restarts WITHOUT it (cutover mirrored only its own staged files)
    11:22:38  pull-sync: "development-vessel: content a9772a7943 -> c1290737f0
              (git 2a5a30567c) — mirroring", then "[mirror-to-live]
              development-vessel mirrored (2a5a305) -> /vessels"
    11:23:10  deployed = 1

So the runtime lags git by at most one pull-sync period — roughly ten minutes — and
then converges by content hash. That is a real window in which a committed change is
not running, and it is worth knowing when reasoning about "did the fix take effect
yet", but it is NOT a divergence that persists or requires intervention. The
content-addressed mirror is doing exactly the job it was hardened for.

WHAT REMAINS, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT MATTERS. Mis-attribution does not self-heal.
Commit 2a5a305 will say "apply recommit-ten-of-eleven-rhythm-families..." forever
while containing an unrelated change to the patcher's logging, and no later tick
repairs a commit message. Every attribution-based question — which gap changed what,
which lane authored it, what a closure predicate should look for, what a bisect will
blame — stays permanently wrong for any commit produced while two composes overlapped
on one vessel. Judge the severity on that, not on the ten-minute mirror lag.

The diagnostic-only rule in repos/development-vessel/src/vacuous-edit.ts refuses an edit that ADDS a log line where the branch previously produced none, while allowing the same information through if it happens to contain a ternary. The carve-out _distinguishesMore compares '?' character counts between added and deleted lines, so a plain console.warn scores 0 > 0 = false and is refused. REPRODUCED against the real function with a negative control: case A (add-a-warn-where-silent) REFUSED; case B (same information plus one '?') ALLOWED. This refused four dispatches of the diagnostic-logging fix for ActivityApiTemplateProvider.getTemplate's silent nulls in repos/ias-executor-ts/src/adapters/activity-api-provider.ts, in BOTH lanes: feature_compose refused it, and the patch_with_tools escalation applied the edit, announced 'verified-green terminal', then emitted FAIL: vacuous_edit. OUTCOME 2026-09-10: a fifth dispatch phrasing the same repair as a 5xx-vs-4xx ternary was composed FAVORABLE and landed as 939bb55 in ias-executor-ts; the warn is live in /vessels and has propagated to consumer dist. So the gate is now WORKED AROUND, NOT FIXED — a plain log added to a silent branch is still refused, and the workaround is only available to an author who knows to smuggle a conditional in. THE FIX IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE: admitting all pure log additions would remove the rule's real value, which is catching a drafter that answers a substantive request with a print statement. The true discriminator is whether the GOAL asked for a diagnostic, and the gate is handed only (before, after) — no diff-local predicate can separate the two. Passing the gap summary into the rule is a change to a compose gate: operator decision, not a patch.

FAILURE DECOMPOSITION (over the corpus while it was still live, 7d, n=1047 deterministic not_achieved): reach failure is NOT diffuse -- 96.2% is a single reason code, deterministic:edit-intent-no-landed-edit (1007). Next largest is 1.1%. So reach is, in practice, the compose funnel's landing rate wearing another name. DETECTOR COVERAGE GAP (law 6): the validator-liveness watchdog shipped 2026-09-09 IS alive (ran 44 min ago, reports SEVERED 38/49) but is structurally blind to this: it flags validators that stopped keeping their own CADENCE, and the reach oracle is DEMAND-DRIVEN -- it fires per dispatch, has no cadence, and therefore cannot be observed as late. A demand-driven validator needs a different liveness predicate: 'N qualifying inputs arrived and produced M verdicts, M/N collapsed', not 'it missed its interval'. UNTESTED HYPOTHESIS, recorded so it is not mistaken for a finding: goals that route via EDIT-INTENT DETECTED -> feature_compose may short-circuit before the reach oracle runs (today's dispatches emitted verdict=FAVORABLE from compose, not a deterministic: reach reason). If edit-intent routing now dominates traffic that alone would starve the oracle. TEST: dispatch one non-edit goal and one edit goal and check whether each produces a 'deterministic:' line. RULED OUT: goal-host commit e673b34 (13:23, the last before the stop) touches only src/registry-field.ts, not the verdict path. CONTROL RUN AFTER FILING -- READ THIS BEFORE OVER-READING THE ABOVE: in the same 60-minute window, activity-api logged 4028 'posterior variant update SKIPPED' events, 3880 of them reason=reach_ungraded, and ZERO applied events. That reads as 'learning has stopped'. IT HAS NOT. posterior-update.ts logs ONLY the skip branch -- there is no APPLIED line -- so the zero is a fact about the logging. Measured at the store instead, variant_performance_metrics shows 41 arms updated in that hour (154 in 24h, 530 in 72h, of 4603 total). Learning is proceeding. Further, 3862 of the 4028 skips (96%) are a SINGLE hot activity, auth_resolve_v1, firing about once per second -- so the skip log is dominated by one retry storm and is not a measure of loop health at all. Two separate items worth their own gaps: (1) auth_resolve_v1 appears to be in a retry loop; (2) a log that emits only on the failure branch cannot be used to compute a rate -- the same defect was found today in patch-with-tools.ts, which logs only FAIL and no success. WHAT SURVIVES: the reach ORACLE is dark (0 deterministic verdicts in 12h, labels 21h stale, 0 /reach grader hits in 12h) and that is independently established. What does NOT follow from it is that the learning loop stopped. PROXIMATE MECHANISM FOUND (2026-09-10T13:30Z): goal walks are failing BEFORE template selection, silently. activeDispatches shows retained dispatches with status='failed', selectedTemplateId=None, executionId=None AND error=None -- including a deliberately simple non-edit probe goal ('report how many shapes are advertised'). recordDeterministicLabel begins 'if (!executionId) return;', so a walk that dies before selection can never produce a verdict, a label, or a goal_execution_paths row. Confirmed at the store: goal_execution_paths rows created in the last 12h = 0, matching learning.goalPathRecorded=false on every retained dispatch. AUTH RULED OUT AS THE CAUSE: vessel writes to activity-api are succeeding -- 12961 execution rows in the last 12h, 2962 of them non-auth -- so this is not a credential failure despite the concurrent auth storm filed separately as a-revoked-credential-retries-once-a-second-and-mints-an-execution-each-time. Activities ARE executing via timers and satisfiers; it is specifically the GOAL WALK that dies early. REGISTRY FINDING, relevance UNPROVEN: discovery holds 10 vessels advertising 406 shapes, and goal-host-vessel is NOT among them (nor are ias-executor, identity, ribosome, boredom, metric-collector, obsidian, federation). That is independently confirmed by the MCP cockpit failing with 'could not find goal-host-vessel via discovery'. Whether the walk's pre-selection failure is caused by this under-population is NOT established and must not be assumed -- the walk runs inside goal-host and does not obviously need goal-host's own registration. NEXT STEP: instrument the pre-selection failure. The dispatch record carries error=None, so the exception or empty-candidate condition is being swallowed; making that reason visible is the whole fix and is a one-line diagnostic at the point where selectedTemplateId is left unset. NOTE the irony and check it first: the vacuous-edit gate filed today as vacuous-gate-refuses-adding-a-log-where-code-was-silent will REFUSE exactly that diagnostic unless it carries a conditional. ROOT CAUSE FOUND. Every 0-step walk logs the same reason -- 85 lines in 12h, all identical: 'opportunistic walk found no applicable pick (empty inferred target)'. The goal->target-shape inference is returning nothing: 'target inference {inferred_target_shapes:[], confidence:0, alternatives:[]}'. Over 24h: 136 EMPTY vs 23 non-empty inferences = 85.5% empty. The 14.5% that infer a target is close to the 10-18% reach rate measured five ways this session, which suggests reach is very largely GATED AT THE FIRST STEP, before any activity is selected or attempted. WHY IT IS EMPTY: inferGoalTargetShapes (repos/goal-host-vessel/src/goal-target-inference.ts) is LLM-backed, and its own docstring at line 212 states 'Returns { shapes: [], confidence: 0, alternatives: [] } on any failure' -- exactly the logged value. LLM providers are currently returning 402 (out of credit) and 429 (rate limited): 40 '402 status code (no body)' plus 27 429s in a 2h window, and 38 'all endpoints exhausted' lines in 12h. TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, DO NOT CONFLATE. (1) The credit/quota exhaustion is an OPERATOR BLOCKER in the CLAUDE.md sense -- missing credentials/funding the substrate cannot fix for itself. (2) The DESIGN DEFECT is independent of credit and survives its repair: a FAILED inference and a genuinely UN-INFERABLE goal return the IDENTICAL value, so the walk cannot tell 'I could not ask' from 'there is no target', and neither can any downstream reader. This is the same class as the silent null in ActivityApiTemplateProvider.getTemplate and the skip-only posterior log -- failure rendered indistinguishable from absence. THE FIX ALREADY EXISTS IN A SIBLING: the deliverable-shapes lookup in index.ts around line 5078 handles this correctly and says so in prose -- 'a failed lookup is not evidence of absence' -- keeping the last known-good vocabulary and logging which case it is in. Target inference should do the same: distinguish transport failure from empty result, keep a last-known-good, and surface the distinction in the log and in the dispatch record.

It currently guesses two filenames and reports the target as untested when neither exists. Extend it so a test that lives under a different filename still counts. One file.

The block to extend begins with this line, which occurs exactly once and is indented with six spaces:
      const candidates = [

Leave the existing two guessed paths and the loop that checks them with access() completely unchanged. They are correct whenever they hit. Add a second chance that runs ONLY if that loop finished without finding anything, so this can never lower the number it reports.

Implement the second chance as simply as possible, using one directory read rather than a hand-written recursive walk:

1. From the target path, which looks like repos/<vessel>/src/<rest>, build the vessel test directory path repos/<vessel>/test, joined onto the same root the existing code already computes.
2. Call readdir on that directory with the recursive option set to true, inside a try so a missing directory simply means no second chance.
3. Keep only entries whose name ends in .test.ts, and stop after the first two hundred.
4. Read each such file and look for the target module being imported.

For step 4 the test is a string containment check against the module basename, and it must match a WHOLE path segment. Build two needles from the basename: a forward slash followed by the basename followed by a double quote, and a forward slash followed by the basename followed by .js and a double quote. Treat the target as covered if a file contains either needle. Repeat both needles with single quotes.

That whole-segment requirement is the point of the change, so do not relax it into a plain substring or prefix test. For a module named gap the specifier ending /gap or /gap.js counts; a specifier ending /gap-lifecycle-scan must not. A prefix test would report coverage for modules a test never loads, and this count feeds the recovery ladder rung that claims landed changes are known to do something, so an over-reporting check makes that rung state something false. Under-reporting is the safe direction here.

Wrap the entire second chance so that any thrown error leaves the result as not covered.

Evidence this is needed: the most frequently rewritten file in this vessel is reported as having no test, while three test files exist whose names begin with its basename, and exactly one of them actually imports it. An import check counts that one and correctly ignores the other two, which a filename check would have miscounted.
