[narrowed from the-newly-failing-gate-attributes-load-sensitive-timeouts-to-the-draft] The newly-failing-test gate blocks correct changes by attributing load-sensitive TIMEOUTS to the draft under review. Its second-run reproduction check cannot tell a timeout apart from a regression, because a slow test stays slow on the retry.

OBSERVED 2026-09-10 on compose route-edit-e2e2e592, a two-line dead-code removal in repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/learning-signal-health-observer.ts that deleted two unused const declarations and nothing else. Both edits applied (apply_failed false), typecheck passed (TC_EXIT=0), shape-dispatch passed (SD_EXIT=0). The verdict was UNFAVORABLE and the semantic gate never even ran (addresses null, reason null). The blocking line was:

    NEW test failures introduced by this draft, REPRODUCED on a second run (1):
    (fail) vessel_mitosis_cutover > freshness gate: refuses cutover when staged_base_sha is missing

THE ATTRIBUTION IS FALSE, AND THE CONTROL IS CHEAP. The edited file is src/resolvers/learning-signal-health-observer.ts; the failing test exercises test/resolvers/vessel-mitosis-cutover.test.ts. There is no import path between them, and the deleted constants were read by nothing. Running that test file on a CLEAN tree with no draft applied reproduces the failure:

    (fail) vessel_mitosis_cutover > freshness gate: refuses cutover when staged_base_sha is missing [5001.02ms]
    (fail) vessel_mitosis_cutover > git-aware cutover: applies staged files, commits, mirrors to /vessels [5001.60ms]
    21 pass, 2 fail

THE MECHANISM IS A TIMEOUT, NOT AN ASSERTION. Both durations are 5001ms against a 5000ms limit. These tests spawn git and filesystem work and are load-sensitive: in a quiet baseline run they pass, and during a compose - which is running typechecks and model calls concurrently, at a host load average around 8 - they exceed the limit. That is why the reproduction check confirms rather than filters them: the second run happens under the same load as the first, so a slow test is slow twice. "Reproduced" is being read as "caused by the draft" when it only establishes "not a one-off flake".

WHY THIS MATTERS. The gate is the last thing standing between a correct change and a landing, and it is rejecting on a signal unrelated to the change. The composer's own hard anchor-failure rate has been measured at 20-23% since 2026-09-08 against a 10-12% baseline; if a share of the remaining verdict losses are false blocks of this kind, effort spent on the drafter and the judge is aimed at the wrong component. It also interacts badly with the fact that this vessel currently carries 28 pre-existing test failures out of 2,235: a noisy baseline makes every comparison less reliable.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. Distinguish a timeout from an assertion failure before attributing it: a test that fails by exceeding its time limit is not evidence about a diff unless the diff plausibly touches its execution path. At minimum, exclude timeout-class failures from newly-failing attribution and report them separately as an environment signal; better, re-run a suspected new failure in isolation, unloaded, before blocking on it, since an isolated re-run is exactly what distinguishes the two. Raising the limit on these specific tests would also work but treats one instance rather than the class.

NOTE THE COMPLEMENTARY DEFECT ALREADY KNOWN. computeNewlyFailing returns NO new failures when the baseline is null or empty, so it fails open in one direction and, as shown here, false-blocks in the other. Both stem from treating a noisy comparison as authoritative.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. Dispatch a provably inert change - for example deleting an unused local - and confirm it is not blocked by a failing test in a file with no import relationship to the edited module. Reading the source cannot establish this; it needs the compose report.

SECOND INSTANCE, 2026-09-10 ~11:40, AND THIS ONE BLOCKED A DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY CHANGE.

Compose route-edit-e40558ea, one op against repos/ias-executor-ts/src/adapters/activity-api-provider.ts. The change adds a single console.warn to a branch that already returns null, so it cannot alter control flow or any value. The compose report records:

    verdict: UNFAVORABLE
    apply_failed: false          <- the edit applied cleanly
    op_count: 1                  <- single operation
    rolled_back: true
    semantic_gate.addresses: null <- the judge NEVER RAN
    summary: "deterministic edit synthesized from the goal's verbatim old→new replacement"

Note the summary: the composer recognised a verbatim old→new pair and synthesized the edit DETERMINISTICALLY, with no model drafting involved. So this is the cleanest possible case — a one-line, machine-synthesized, provably inert diagnostic — and it was still refused, before any semantic judgement, by the gate that precedes it.

WHY THIS INSTANCE MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIRST. The change being blocked is the one that makes this class of failure diagnosable at all: it adds the missing log line to ActivityApiTemplateProvider.getTemplate, whose silent nulls are why a template that activity-api serves with HTTP 200 is reported by goal-host as absent, and why that investigation took seven hypotheses. So the test gate is currently blocking the instrumentation needed to diagnose a separate defect - a false block with a compounding cost, not merely a wasted draft.

TWO ATTEMPTS, SAME OUTCOME. Dispatched twice, roughly forty minutes apart, both reaching fc-plan and neither producing a semantic verdict. That rules out a one-off: whatever the gate is comparing against is failing this diff consistently, and consistently for reasons unrelated to the diff, which is exactly the failure mode this gap describes.

THE SECOND INSTANCE IS NOT A TIMEOUT — IT IS A CORRUPTED TEST TREE, AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT AND WORSE MECHANISM.

Reading the verify block of route-edit-e40558ea rather than assuming it matched the first instance:

    compose environment:   134 pass, 32 fail, 30 ERRORS, 166 tests across 46 files
    clean tree, same repo:  372 pass, 23 fail,  0 errors, 395 tests across 50 files

The compose ran FEWER FILES (46 vs 50) and produced 30 ERRORS. Errors at that count are module-load failures, not assertion failures and not timeouts. A one-line console.warn added to a branch that already returns null cannot remove four test files from a run or prevent modules from loading.

The gate's own message names the symptom precisely — "PASSING TESTS DISAPPEARED: 353 -> 134 (a draft must not delete coverage or break module load to go green)" — and that rule is CORRECT. A draft really must not delete coverage. The defect is the attribution: the coverage vanished for a reason the draft did not cause, and the gate has no way to tell the difference.

THE LIKELY CAUSE TIES THIS TO THE CONCURRENT-COMPOSE CLASS. Composes share working trees; this substrate has already recorded both directions of that contention — "SKIPPING ROLLBACK ... file content has changed (likely by another concurrent compose)" on the refusal side, and a cutover committing another gap's staged edit under its own attribution on the landing side. A third consequence follows directly: another compose's IN-FLIGHT, HALF-APPLIED edit sitting in the shared tree while this draft's suite runs will break module load for whatever files import it, and every one of those failures is then attributed to the draft under test.

That converts an intermittent nuisance into a systematic one. It is not load-sensitive and not random: it fires whenever two composes overlap on one vessel, which on a continuously-running lane is most of the time. It also explains why two attempts forty minutes apart failed identically — not a flake reproducing, but a shared tree that was dirty on both occasions.

NOTE ALSO: the clean tree carries 23 pre-existing failures of its own. So the baseline this gate differences against is noisy even before contention, which is the condition the original entry above describes.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY, REVISED. Run the same provably-inert one-line diff twice: once while no other compose touches that vessel, and once during a concurrent compose on it. If the first passes and the second reports vanished coverage, the attribution defect is contention, not flake, and the fix is isolation of the test tree rather than better flake filtering.

[narrowed from a-cutover-commits-another-gaps-staged-edit-under-its-own-attribution] A compose cutover for one gap committed another gap's staged edit under its own attribution, and mirrored only its own files — leaving the swept-in change present in git and absent from the running tree.

OBSERVED 2026-09-10 11:11:17. An operator dispatch edited repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/patch-with-tools.ts, adding a diagnostic to the semantic gate's PASSED log line. It reached origin/dev inside commit 2a5a305, whose message is "substrate-authored: apply recommit-ten-of-eleven-rhythm-families-have-no-staleness-driver-syntax_break-compose-report via mitosis cutover" — a completely unrelated gap about rhythm staleness drivers. `git log -S` confirms 2a5a305 is the commit that introduced the line; the operator's own dispatch produced no commit of its own.

TWO DISTINCT DEFECTS, BOTH FOLLOWING FROM THE SAME CAUSE.

  1. MIS-ATTRIBUTED LANDING. The commit says it applies the rhythm-families gap and
     in fact carries an unrelated change to the patcher's logging. Anyone asking
     "what did this gap change?" — an operator, a closure predicate, the gap store's
     own durability accounting, a future bisect — gets a wrong answer. Worse, the
     compose that owns the commit never judged the change it carried: the semantic
     gate that ran, ran against the rhythm-families patch.

  2. GIT AHEAD OF RUNTIME. The cutover mirrored its own staged files to /vessels and
     not the swept-in one. Measured immediately after: origin/dev contains the line,
     /vessels/development-vessel/src/resolvers/patch-with-tools.ts does not, and the
     vessel restarted at 11:11:36 — after the 11:11:17 commit — so the restart did
     not carry it either. The runtime is behind git for that file until the next
     pull-sync reconciles it.

THIS IS THE CONCURRENT-COMPOSE CLASS IN THE LANDING DIRECTION. The same root cause is
already recorded on the refusal side: "SKIPPING ROLLBACK ... file content has changed
(likely by another concurrent compose)", where a refused compose's bytes survive
because another compose touched the file. Here the same shared-tree contention runs
forward instead of backward: whichever compose reaches cutover first commits whatever
is in the tree, including work it did not author and did not gate.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. Every accounting this substrate keeps about its own
self-modification is attribution-based — which gap closed, which compose landed, which
lane authored what. Commit attribution is the substrate's ONLY durable record of that,
and it is wrong whenever two composes overlap on one vessel. It also silently defeats
the one-operation-per-plan discipline that the partial-landing evidence recommends: a
plan can be atomic and still arrive inside someone else's commit.

summary:
The recovery ladder's second rung, which asserts that nothing lands unread, broke at 15:39 on 2026-09-10 and cannot be diagnosed from anything the system records.

WHAT BROKE. The rung requires every staged artifact to have a checker that reads it, and it is deliberately stricter than its siblings: one unread artifact breaks it. It now reports 1303 examined and exactly 1 unexamined out of 1304, a fraction of 0.9992.

THE CAUSE IS A TRUNCATED PATH. The offending execution is a compose at 15:34:43 whose examination breakdown by extension reads a single entry for the extension dot t. There is no checker registered for that extension, so the artifact counted as unread. A search of both the vessel clones and the super-repo finds NO file anywhere whose name ends in dot t. The extension regex is correct and would capture dot ts from a normal TypeScript path, so the staged path itself arrived truncated by one character, and the truncation happened upstream of the examination split.

WHY IT CANNOT BE DIAGNOSED. The split already records the identity of every unread file. The result type carries an unexamined_files list, and its own comment states the field exists so that a passing static check can never again mean passed for a file nothing opened. That list is not propagated into the execution trace: the trace carries only the counts and the extension histogram. Every compose report on disk carries an empty list. So the rung can say that something landed unread and cannot say what, which makes the break unactionable and the truncation invisible.

THIS IS THE COMPUTED-THEN-DISCARDED PATTERN. The information needed to act exists, is produced at the right layer, and is dropped before it reaches any consumer. The same shape has been recorded elsewhere in this substrate for verified-unique anchors that are computed and thrown away.

PROPOSED CHANGE, in the file named by edit_site: carry the unexamined file list into the trace metadata alongside the counts, bounded to a small number of entries so a large staging set cannot bloat a row. That turns a bare count into a name, which is the difference between a rung that reports a problem and a rung that can be acted on. The truncation itself is a second defect and cannot be located until the name is available.

FALSIFIER. Break the rung deliberately by staging an artifact with an extension no checker handles, then read the resulting trace. The gap is closed when the trace names the file rather than only counting it. Today it counts only.

summary:
[narrowed from enumerated-anchor-choice-is-wired-only-to-the-path-the-failures-do-not-take] The enumerated-anchor mechanism that makes a fabricated anchor impossible exists in this file and is wired only to the path the failures do not take. Extending it to the primary drafting path is the single highest-leverage change available to the authoring lane.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS. In the re-derivation block, feature-compose.ts offers the model a numbered list of verified-unique anchors and takes the bytes from OUR list rather than from the model's output. Its own comment states the principle: "let it pick an INDEX and take the bytes from the verified list here. The anchor then CANNOT be invented, because the model never writes it." That block also handles the details correctly — an indexed answer wins over free text, the window-provenance check is deliberately skipped for an indexed anchor because such an anchor has better provenance than the window test, a single-candidate list is auto-accepted, and every check fails open.

WHERE IT IS NOT. The identifier `anchor_index` occurs at exactly four lines in this file, ALL inside that re-derivation block. The PRIMARY drafting path still asks the model to reproduce an anchor as text: it logs "[fc-anchors] supplied verified-unique anchors for <path> (N locator candidate(s))" and then requests a verbatim old_string. The drafter demonstrably paraphrases what it is shown — measured on src/seed/index.ts, an untouched file: the source has `export const SEED_TEMPLATES: ActivityTemplate[] = [` and the model returned it without the type annotation; the source has `export { X } from "./add-resolver-to-vessel.js";` and the model returned it without the from-clause. Indentation is altered the same way.

PROMPT-LEVEL CORRECTION HAS BEEN TRIED AND DOES NOT WORK ON THIS CLASS. Commit 12c4c58 added an explicit instruction not to return the failed anchor, and the very next repair echoed it anyway. The re-derivation comment reaches the same conclusion independently: "A model that ignores a list will ignore a longer one, so stop asking it to reproduce a string at all." The lever must be mechanical.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING. Hard anchor failure (apply_failed with ops_applied == 0) accounts for roughly 28% of compose attempts, and the composer's own rate has sat at 20-23% since 2026-09-08 against a 10-12% baseline on 09-05/06. This is the dominant loss in the authoring lane.

SHAPE OF THE CHANGE. Two sites must move together, which is why it has not happened incrementally: the drafting prompt must render the verified-unique anchors as an INDEXED list with an instruction to answer with an index, and the plan-application path must resolve an op's anchor_index against that same list before falling back to op.old_string. Both halves must be in one change; a prompt that offers indices to an applier that ignores them is worse than neither, because the model will spend its answer on a field that is dropped.

DO NOT THREAD THE LIST THROUGH FUNCTION SIGNATURES. Two prior attempts on this file died on cross-scope bindings (TS2339, TS2304) and one on changing a return type without changing its declaration (TS2322: returning {text, conceptIds} from a function still declared Promise<string>). Use a module-scoped array holding the last rendered anchor list for the file being planned, written where the list is built and read where the op is applied. Anchor every edit on a single short line; measured landing on this file collapses as anchor length grows.

FAIL OPEN, AND CHANGE NOTHING ELSE. An absent, non-numeric or out-of-range index must fall through to today's exact behaviour, so the change can only add a path and never remove one. Preserve the existing uniqueness check and refuseRederivedEdit call unchanged.

VERIFY BEHAVIOURALLY. The claim is not that the code contains a new identifier. It is that the hard anchor-failure rate falls. compose-drift-tick already measures exactly this population (apply_failed AND ops_applied == 0 over feature_compose executions, day-scale) against the composer's own median baseline, so the closure test is a sustained fall in that rate on complete days after the change lands, with the day the change landed recorded. Note this file has NO TEST FILE, so every gate reads the diff and none executes it; a FAVORABLE verdict here means reviewed, not run.

summary:
The recovery ladder's second rung holds only when the all-time sum of unexamined staged artifacts is exactly zero. That sum can only increase, so the rung is a one-way latch: the first artifact that ever lands unread breaks it permanently, and no amount of subsequent correct behaviour can restore it.

THE MECHANISM. The rung reads a sum over every execution carrying the examination metadata, with no time bound, and its holding condition is that the unexamined count equals zero. Both halves are necessary for the latch. A sum with no window never decreases, and an equality against zero admits no recovery. One event at 15:34:43 on 2026-09-10 pushed that sum from zero to one, and the ladder moved from six rungs holding to five, with the first break shifting from the third rung to the second.

WHY THE STRICTNESS IS OTHERWISE RIGHT. The rung is deliberately stricter than its siblings, and the reasoning in the source is sound: an unexamined artifact is not a weak signal but the absence of one, and this substrate has already landed a database-breaking migration through exactly that hole. Requiring zero unread artifacts is the correct standard for CURRENT behaviour. The defect is not the strictness, it is applying an all-time accumulator to a present-tense question, which converts a strict standard into an unreachable one.

CONSEQUENCE. From 15:34:43 onward the ladder can never report all rungs holding, whatever the system does next. A measure that cannot represent recovery cannot be used to judge whether recovery happened, and a permanently broken rung will be read as noise within days and then ignored, which costs the substrate the one strict check it has on artifacts landing unread.

COMPARE THE THIRD RUNG, which has the same shape in a milder form: it averages over all history rather than summing, so it recovers, but only after hundreds of further observations. Both rungs answer present-tense questions with all-time accumulators. The second is the absolute case.

PROPOSED CHANGE, for a reviewer rather than the reporter. Bound the window to recent executions while keeping the zero requirement inside it, so the standard stays strict and the rung can return to holding once the fleet is again reading every artifact it stages. Report the all-time count alongside as history rather than as the verdict.

DECLARED CONFLICT. The operator reporting this is working under a directive to bring every rung to holding, so a change that unlatches this rung would directly serve that goal. It is filed rather than made for that reason. The same abstention was applied to the third rung's windowing question, and in that case a measurement showed the change would not in fact have helped, which is why the abstention is worth keeping rather than reasoning around.

FALSIFIER. After any change, stage an artifact with an extension no checker handles, confirm the rung breaks, then run a period of correct composes and confirm the rung returns to holding. Today the second half is impossible by construction.

Find these three consecutive lines (each occurs exactly once in the file):
      count("SELECT count() FROM execution WHERE metadata.examination_examined != NONE GROUP ALL;"),
      count("SELECT math::sum(metadata.examination_examined) AS count FROM execution WHERE metadata.examination_examined != NONE GROUP ALL;"),
      count("SELECT math::sum(metadata.examination_unexamined) AS count FROM execution WHERE metadata.examination_examined != NONE GROUP ALL;"),

Replace them with these three lines:
      count("SELECT count() FROM execution WHERE metadata.examination_examined != NONE AND executed_at > time::now() - 24h GROUP ALL;"),
      count("SELECT math::sum(metadata.examination_examined) AS count FROM execution WHERE metadata.examination_examined != NONE AND executed_at > time::now() - 24h GROUP ALL;"),
      count("SELECT math::sum(metadata.examination_unexamined) AS count FROM execution WHERE metadata.examination_examined != NONE AND executed_at > time::now() - 24h GROUP ALL;"),

The only change is inserting" AND executed_at > time::now() - 24h" before" GROUP ALL;" in each of the three queries. Change nothing else, no other line, and no other file.

WHY. Rung 2 asks a present-tense question: "Does anything land unexamined?" It answers it with an unwindowed all-time math::sum(metadata.examination_unexamined) and holds only when that sum equals exactly 0. A sum over all history is monotone non-decreasing, so once any single execution records one unexamined file the rung reports broken permanently, no matter how the system behaves afterward. That has already happened: the sum went from 0 to 1 at 15:34:43 today, from one execution whose staged path had been truncated. After that first trip the rung reports the same value regardless of system state, so it has stopped being a measurement. The ladder can never read 7 of 7 by its own arithmetic. All three queries are windowed together rather than only the unexamined sum, because the rung also reports staged_examined and an examined_fraction derived from these numbers; windowing one and not the others would report a 24-hour numerator against an all-time denominator.

DECLARED CONFLICT. This change is proposed by the same operator whose work rung 2 grades, so it deserves scrutiny rather than deference. Two facts bound the risk. First, it cannot improve today's verdict: the windowed query was executed read-only against the live database before this dispatch and still returns unexamined = 1, examined = 365 over 24 hours, so rung 2 continues to report broken exactly as it does now. It can only clear roughly 24 hours after the truncation event, and only if no further unexamined file appears. Second, the underlying defect that produced the single unexamined file has already been repaired and deployed in gap-to-feature.ts, so what the windowed rung will measure tomorrow is whether that repair actually held. A change that cannot flatter the party proposing it today, and that can only report clean after a full window of genuinely clean behavior, is an instrument repair rather than a weakened threshold. The holds condition stays exactly as it is: the sum must still be zero.

Rung 3 is deliberately left alone. Its covered_fraction is also all-time but it is rising on its own, from 0.3606 to 0.4199 across today, so it can still observe repair and needs no intervention. Only rung 2 is permanently pinned.

summary:
In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts, make the grounding-visibility check require a path boundary instead of a bare substring match.

The file contains exactly one occurrence of this fragment, on line 3787:
if (grounding.includes(base)) continue; // visible in the window → groundable, fine

Replace it with exactly this:
if (new RegExp("/" + base.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&") + "(?![A-Za-z0-9])").test(grounding)) continue; // visible in the window → groundable, fine

One file, one op. Change nothing else.

WHY. That check decides whether a target file is visible in the grounding window, and it uses plain substring containment on the basename. Two false positives follow, both verified by executing the old and new expressions against a grounding window containing learning-signal-health-observer.ts and operational-state.ts:

- A TRUNCATED path is a prefix of its real form. Basename learning-signal-health-observer.t (a real path that lost its final character) is a substring of learning-signal-health-observer.ts, so the old check reports it visible and groundable even though no such file exists. This is not hypothetical: it happened on gap route-edit-098185ac today, and the resulting compose examined 0 of 1 staged files and broke rung 2 of the operational_state ladder.
- A SHORT generic basename matches a longer unrelated file. Basename state.ts is a substring of operational-state.ts, so any target named state.ts is reported visible on the strength of a completely different file.

Measured with the four cases above: the old expression returns true for ALL FOUR, including the two that must be false. The new expression returns false, true, false, true, which is correct in every case. The leading slash forces the match to start at a path segment boundary, so state.ts no longer matches operational-state.ts, and the trailing (?![A-Za-z0-9]) forces it to end at one, so observer.t no longer matches observer.ts.

THIS DOES NOT FAIL CLOSED, which the comment above this block explicitly warns against. The check only decides whether to SKIP the per-target existence probe below it. A target that is no longer considered visible simply falls through to that probe; if the file does not exist it is still treated as a net-new create and allowed, exactly as before. Nothing that previously proceeded as a creation is blocked. The only behavior that changes is that a target which merely looked visible because its name is a prefix or a substring of some other file is now actually checked.

In repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/feature-compose.ts, repair a corrupted regex-escape call on line 3787.

A previous edit to this line was applied incorrectly: the anchor text of that edit was substituted into the replacement argument where the escape placeholder should have been. The file now contains exactly one occurrence of this fragment:
base.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\\]\]/g, "\\if (grounding.includes(base)) continue; // visible in the window → groundable, fine")

Replace that fragment with exactly this:
base.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, (c) => "\\" + c)

One file, one op. Everything else on the line, including the surrounding new RegExp(...) call, the leading "/", the trailing "(?![A-Za-z0-9])", the .test(grounding) and the trailing comment, stays exactly as it is.

WHY. The intent of that call is to escape regex metacharacters in a filename before embedding it in a RegExp. As it stands, two things are wrong. The character class reads [.*+?^${}()|[\\]\] which matches a metacharacter only when it is immediately followed by a right square bracket, and the replacement is a long literal sentence rather than the matched character. For ordinary basenames nothing matches, so the call is currently a no-op and the surrounding check behaves correctly by accident; but a filename containing a bracket would splice that entire sentence into the pattern.

The replacement uses a function replacer, (c) => "\\" + c, rather than the $& placeholder. That is deliberate: $& is what was misread as a substitution slot last time, and a function replacer cannot be confused for one.

Verified by execution against a grounding window containing learning-signal-health-observer.ts and operational-state.ts. The new form returns false for basename learning-signal-health-observer.t, true for learning-signal-health-observer.ts, false for state.ts, and true for operational-state.ts, which is correct in all four cases, and it does not throw for the bracket-bearing names weird].ts and a.b].ts or for x+y.ts.

A daily in-process timer inside a process whose mean lifetime is 11 minutes can never fire. The interval path is therefore dead by construction, and with the boot gate closed the selector has no live path at all.

MEASURED: a mitosis cutover can leave a change STAGED-BUT-NOT-COMMITTED in a vessel's git worktree while that change is simultaneously LIVE in the runtime. Observed 2026-09-10T20:38Z for repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/gap-to-feature.ts: git status reports 'M ' (staged, index modified), HEAD does not contain the change (git show HEAD:<path> | grep -c returns 0), git log -S with a pathspec returns NO commit, and yet /vessels/development-vessel/src/resolvers/gap-to-feature.ts contains it. The cutover logged its freshness check passing (freshnessOK=true, staged_base_sha == current_live_sha, net_new=false) and then did not commit. WHY THIS IS DANGEROUS AND NOT MERELY UNTIDY: for vessels that run from src (bun run src/index.ts), the WORKING TREE IS THE RUNTIME ARTIFACT. So the change is in effect but has no durable record. Any baseline restore, git checkout, or compose rollback silently reverts it, and because nothing was ever committed there is no evidence it existed. This is not hypothetical: TWICE today a landed edit vanished this way. The recordDeterministicLabel call site added to the early edit-intent path (commit 1db4415) disappeared from the live file during a crash-recovery baseline restore, and was only detected because a later grep returned 0 where 1 was expected. DETECTION THAT WORKS, use it: `git log -S "<verbatim fragment>" --oneline -- <path>` inside the vessel's worktree. An empty result means the change is NOT in history regardless of what the file or the compose report says. Checking the file, the compose verdict, or /vessels alone cannot distinguish 'landed' from 'staged and about to evaporate'. WHAT DETECTS THE CLASS WITHOUT AN OPERATOR (law 6): a post-cutover assertion that, for every path the cutover claims to have applied, the path appears in HEAD -- not in the worktree. The cutover already computes staged_base_sha and current_live_sha for its freshness check, so the comparison is available at the same site; what is missing is an assertion AFTER the commit step that the commit actually happened. A cutover that stages and returns success is reporting on its own intent rather than its effect. CURRENT STATE: the staged change is the recommit landability penalty (a scored -0.15 down-weight for recommit lineages in landabilityScore). It is live in the runtime path but NOT loaded, because development-vessel runs from src and has not restarted since. Restart was deliberately deferred: two composes were in flight and restarting would have aborted them, possibly including the cutover that would commit this very change. ⚠ RETRACTION AND RE-FRAMING, same session. The headline claim above -- that the cutover staged the change and did NOT commit it -- is WRONG. It committed asynchronously as 9b305d2 a few minutes later; git status is now clean for that path and git log -S returns the commit. I sampled during the window and read a slow step as a failed one. That is the same error class as reading a resting state as a terminal one, which my own operator scorecard already lists as my most frequent mistake. WHAT SURVIVES, and it is narrower but still real: there is a WINDOW between staging and committing during which the change is live in the runtime (for vessels that run from src, the working tree IS the runtime artifact) while having no durable record. A baseline restore landing inside that window reverts the change and leaves no evidence it ever existed. That is not hypothetical -- commit 1db4415 (the recordDeterministicLabel early-path call site) was lost exactly this way earlier the same day, detected only because a later grep returned 0 where 1 was expected. SO THE DEFECT IS NOT 'the cutover fails to commit'. It is that NOTHING DETECTS A SILENT REVERT. A change can be applied, observed live, and then removed by an unrelated recovery path, with every report still saying it landed. WHAT DETECTS THE CLASS (law 6), revised: not a post-commit assertion inside the cutover -- that would only re-check work the cutover already completes correctly. The gap is a POST-LAND VERIFIER that re-reads a landed change some time AFTER the cutover returns and asserts the fragment is still present in HEAD. Cheap, needs only the path and a verbatim fragment both already recorded in the compose report, and it is the only thing that would have caught the 1db4415 loss without an operator happening to grep. DETECTION RECIPE, unchanged and still the right one: git log -S "<verbatim fragment>" --oneline -- <path> inside the vessel worktree. But run it LATER, not immediately -- an empty result right after a cutover may simply mean the commit has not happened yet.

A previous edit to this line was applied incorrectly: the anchor text of that edit was substituted into the replacement argument where the escape placeholder should have been. The file now contains exactly one occurrence of this fragment:
base.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\\]\]/g, "\\if (grounding.includes(base)) continue; // visible in the window → groundable, fine")

Replace that fragment with exactly this:
base.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, (c) => "\\" + c)

One file, one op. Everything else on the line, including the surrounding new RegExp(...) call, the leading "/", the trailing "(?![A-Za-z0-9])", the .test(grounding) and the trailing comment, stays exactly as it is.

WHY. The intent of that call is to escape regex metacharacters in a filename before embedding it in a RegExp. As it stands, two things are wrong. The character class reads [.*+?^${}()|[\\]\] which matches a metacharacter only when it is immediately followed by a right square bracket, and the replacement is a long literal sentence rather than the matched character. For ordinary basenames nothing matches, so the call is currently a no-op and the surrounding check behaves correctly by accident; but a filename containing a bracket would splice that entire sentence into the pattern.

The replacement uses a function replacer, (c) => "\\" + c, rather than the $& placeholder. That is deliberate: $& is what was misread as a substitution slot last time, and a function replacer cannot be confused for one.

Verified by execution against a grounding window containing learning-signal-health-observer.ts and operational-state.ts. The new form returns false for basename learning-signal-health-observer.t, true for learning-signal-health-observer.ts, false for state.ts, and true for operational-state.ts, which is correct in all four cases, and it does not throw for the bracket-bearing names weird].ts and a.b].ts or for x+y.ts.

CHANGE: repos/development-vessel/src/resolvers/gap-to-feature.ts, landabilityScore now applies a flat -0.15 penalty to any gap whose id matches /(^|-)recommit-/i. Landed as commit 9b305d2, live in /vessels, development-vessel restarted 2026-09-10T20:50:43Z to load it. ONE change only; nothing else was altered in that function. WHY: landabilityScore ranks open gaps for the compose lane and was blind to recommit lineage. It already penalises stale-proposal / demand-trace / forward-chain / backlog / unknown id patterns on the preceding line, but a recommit gap is filed under a NEW id (recommit-<gap.id>-<cls>), so its failed_attempts starts at 0 and the retry penalty further down never fires. A retry of a known failure was scored exactly like fresh work. PRE-MEASUREMENT, matched 3-day window, landings counted at the git layer (the consuming layer, not the compose report): non-recommit 76 landings / 283 attempts = 26.9%; recommit depth-1 6 / 113 = 5.3%; recommit depth-2 4 / 18 = 22.2%. Recommit was ~31.6% of all compose attempts and returned 11.6% of landings, against an open-gap backlog of ~423. Immediate pre-change baseline over the last 60 compose reports: recommit 18/60 = 30.0%. HYPOTHESIS: down-weighting recommit in selection reallocates lane capacity toward the backlog, which converts at 26.9%, and should net MORE landings per unit capacity -- not fewer, despite recommit itself landing less often. DESIGN CHOICES AND THE EVIDENCE THAT FORCED THEM: (a) a SCORED down-weight, not a gate, so recommit still runs when the pool is thin and keeps the 11.6% of landings it earns; (b) FLAT, not depth-scaled -- depth-2 measured 22.2%, no worse than fresh work, so penalising depth harder would contradict the data; (c) NOT a per-class ban -- every failure class recommits to a nonzero yield (semantic_reject 9.8%, anchor_not_found 10.3%, syntax_break 4.8%, typecheck 15%, verify_failed 23%), so there is no dead class to prune and banning one would have been a wrong mint. POST-MEASUREMENT NOT YET POSSIBLE, and this is a wall-clock limit rather than a result: the compose lane runs at roughly 5 attempts/hour, so a sample large enough to move a proportion needs HOURS. At the time of writing, n=1 new compose report since the marker -- meaningless. HOW TO COMPLETE THIS EXPERIMENT: the marker timestamp is stored in the container at /tmp/penalty-marker (2026-09-10 20:50:43 UTC). Run: find /workspace/proposals -name '*compose-report.json' -newermt "$(cat /tmp/penalty-marker)" and compute the recommit share of the basenames. Compare against the 30.0% pre-change baseline. Then re-measure reach over goal_verification_labels for the same window. ⚠ DO NOT read a fall in recommit SHARE as success on its own. The share falling is the mechanism working, not the outcome. The outcome is LANDINGS PER UNIT CAPACITY, and it must be counted at the git layer with git log -S and a pathspec -- the compose report is not evidence a change landed, as this session established repeatedly. If recommit share falls AND total landings/hour does not rise, the hypothesis is wrong and the penalty should be reverted, not tuned.

A query whose WHERE clause matches the prefix of the composite index idx_trace_digest_activity_success_time on trace_digest fields activity_id, success, executed_at returns zero rows with status OK while each conjunct alone returns hundreds. Measured with EXPLAIN on the live database 2026-09-10: WHERE activity_id = X AND success = true produces plan index idx_trace_digest_activity_success_time, operator union, value empty-list, which iterates nothing; WHERE activity_id = X alone produces operator = with the value and returns 368 rows. Equality against the indexed boolean fails in both directions: AND success = true and AND success = false both return empty, while AND success != false returns 344, AND success returns 344, AND success != true returns 35 and AND !success returns 35. No error is raised in any case. Impact measured: this silently emptied the entire extraction stage of the learning loop. The exemplar selector reported processed 101 and failed 0 while execution_exemplar held 0 rows, because its per-activity query is exactly the broken conjunction. Two code-level workarounds have been landed in repos/activity-api/src/services/exemplar-selector.ts replacing the equality forms with inequality forms. Those are workarounds, not a fix: any other query in any vessel that filters this table by activity_id together with an equality on success will silently return nothing. The durable repair is a schema-level change applied as a migration, for example dropping or redefining the composite index, or a SurrealDB version upgrade if this is a known planner defect. Predicate for closure: run EXPLAIN on SELECT id FROM trace_digest WHERE activity_id = X AND success = true and verify the plan is not operator union with an empty value list, and that the query returns the same count as the equivalent inequality form.

Nothing in the substrate asks whether a store that should be filling is empty. execution_exemplar held 0 rows for the entire life of the system while its input trace_digest held 1181 rows, and no check, report, or gap ever surfaced it. It was found by hand on 2026-09-10 while answering an unrelated design question. Two independent defects had to be repaired before a single row could be written, and the first one hid the second: the boot run was gated on an env var that is set nowhere and the only other path was a 24 hour in-process setInterval inside a process whose mean uptime is 11.4 minutes, so the job had never executed; once it did execute it reported processed 101 and failed 0 and still wrote nothing, because its per-activity query hits a composite-index planner defect that returns zero rows with status OK. Neither defect was visible to any existing instrument, and the worker log actively misreported: processed 101, failed 0, receiver 0. The proposed detector is deliberately mechanism-independent, because the two causes here were completely unrelated and a scheduling audit would have caught only one of them: for each store that has a designated writer, is the store empty while its input is non-empty? That single question catches a dead timer, a closed env gate, a query-planner defect, a schemafull discard, a wrong-table read and a permissions denial identically, and it costs one query per pair. This should be minted as an activity so Thompson can grade it, scheduled on the timer tier rather than by the learner it audits, emitting a report shape and filing a gap per empty pair. It must not be scheduled by the selection mechanism it observes: the rhythm conductor precedent shows a validator whose own scheduling drifted took 90 of 102 validators dormant with it. Predicate for closure: a report shape exists that enumerates writer-store pairs with their input and output row counts, it names at least one pair, and re-running it against the state of 2026-09-10 would have flagged execution_exemplar 0 against trace_digest 1181.

summary:
In repos/activity-api/src/services/exemplar-selector.ts, change the remaining broken query predicate so the failure-side exemplar query stops silently returning zero rows.

The file contains exactly one occurrence of this fragment:
AND success = false ORDER BY executed_at DESC LIMIT $n

Replace it with exactly this:
AND success != true ORDER BY executed_at DESC LIMIT $n

One file, one op. Change nothing else on that line, no other line, and no other file.

WHY. This is the companion to the success-side repair already landed on the line above, which changed success = true to success != false for the same reason.

trace_digest carries a composite index, idx_trace_digest_activity_success_time, on fields activity_id, success, executed_at. This query is exactly that index's prefix, and on the equality form the planner compiles it to an empty key set. Measured with EXPLAIN on the live database: WHERE activity_id = X AND success = true produces plan index idx_trace_digest_activity_success_time, operator union, value [], which iterates nothing and returns status OK with zero rows, while WHERE activity_id = X alone produces operator = with the value and returns 368 rows.

Equality against the indexed boolean fails in both directions. Verified counts for activity_id validator-dispatch: AND success = false returns empty, while AND success != true returns 35 and AND !success returns 35. The inequality form returns the correct rows with ORDER BY and LIMIT still applied.

success != true selects exactly the rows where success is false, because the field is declared TYPE bool with ASSERT $value != NONE, so it can never be null or absent. The meaning is unchanged.

Consequence of leaving it: the exemplar selector reports processed 101 and failed 0 while writing no failure exemplars at all, so the extraction stage of the learning loop keeps only successes and never the counter-examples it is supposed to retain.

This is a targeted workaround for a query-planner defect, not a semantic change.

The intent of that VALUE clause is to default the timestamp when the caller omits it, but on this INSERT INTO form the default does not apply, so the field arrives NONE and fails the datetime type check. Supplying the value explicitly satisfies the declared type and makes the default irrelevant rather than relying on it.

This is the third defect in the same stage, each of which hid the next. First the job never ran at all: its boot run was gated on an env var set nowhere, and its only other path was a 24 hour in-process interval inside a process whose mean uptime is 11.4 minutes. Once it ran, its per-activity query silently returned zero rows because the query matched a composite index prefix that the planner compiles to an empty key set. With that repaired the insert loop finally executes, which is how these type failures became visible at all: the warnings are logged from inside the loop, so before the query was fixed there was nothing to log.
